20019-lectures-on-landscape-delivered-at:
John Ruskin delivered his Lectures on Landscape at Oxford in Lent term 1871. He compares two Turner paintings by their harmony of color. One is a harmony of cool color, the other of hot. Both are exquisitely designed in ornamental lines, he grants. But they were not painted for those qualities, he insists. One scene is full of delight to men; the other, of pain and danger. Turner's object is the human meaning of landscape.

Ruskin was Oxford's first Slade Professor of Fine Art. His lectures drew crowds and set Victorian taste. Landscape here means truth to nature, morally read. These talks teach students how to see before judging. Turner stands as prophet of that seeing throughout. The lectures remain a gateway into Ruskin's mind.
20765-diary-of-anna-green-winslow-a-bost:
Alice Morse Earle edited the diary of Anna Green Winslow, a Boston schoolgirl of 1771. Anna was sent from Nova Scotia to Boston, her parents' birthplace, to be finished at good schools. She wrote with care, both for her parents' joy and for practice in fine handwriting.

Daily life in colonial Boston fills the small pages: lessons, calls, dress, and church. A girl's eye catches what grand histories miss. The diary shows the prim, narrow round of a town on the edge of revolt. Few sources let young readers hear the past in a voice so close to their own age.
arxiv-2510-00071:
Dongqi Zheng wrote this 2025 paper on making large reasoning models cheaper to run. Such models often think far longer than a problem needs, wasting time, tokens, and energy. Zheng proposes Adaptive Reasoning Suppression, a method that watches a model's growing certainty as it works. When the model looks sure enough, the method trims the extra reasoning steps. The method needs no new training of the model itself.

Zheng tested the method on math reasoning tasks across several model designs. It cut token use by up to about half in the best cases. It also cut delay and energy use by large shares, while accuracy held steady or improved. Fixed cut-off rules did worse, because the method adjusts to each model's own path. The work matters for anyone paying to run reasoning models at scale.
arxiv-2510-00171:
Sreetama Das, Gian Luca Giorgi, and Roberta Zambrini published this 2025 paper on quantum reservoir computing. A reservoir computer lets a fixed, untrained system process signals over time, and only the readout is trained. Their system pairs one qubit with one bosonic mode, following the classic Jaynes-Cummings model of light and matter. They also test its dispersive limit, where the pair interacts more gently.

Both reservoirs were benchmarked on memory tasks that mix straight recall with nonlinear mixing. Unusually, the systems remembered nonlinear patterns better than simple linear ones. On the Mackey-Glass series, a standard chaotic forecasting test, they predicted comparably to known methods. Watching higher-order signals from the boson and slicing time into channels both boosted performance. The authors present the pair as a small, tunable building block for quantum machine learning hardware.
arxiv-2510-00271:
Nicole Crumpler and three colleagues published this 2025 astronomy paper hunting ultra-light dark matter through dead stars. If dark matter particles are extremely light, they form waves with a long coherence length. Such a field could swell or shrink white dwarfs in a spatially correlated pattern. The team asked whether catalog data could reveal that telltale correlation scale.

They first simulated the hunt, including dust, binaries, envelope differences, and noisy measurements. Only radius shifts near ten percent would stand out above that realistic noise, they found. Applying their routine to a Sloan survey catalog of more than ten thousand white dwarfs did show a correlation. Its scale sat near three hundred parsecs, with a striking average significance. Careful checks, though, traced the signal to biases in cool, nearby white dwarf measurements. The authors report a null result and a method ready for better data.
arxiv-2510-00471:
Yankai Jiang and three colleagues published this 2025 paper on the water footprint of supercomputing, an overlooked cost of big computation. High-performance systems drink water twice: directly for cooling and indirectly through power generation. Carbon emissions get the headlines, while water use stays largely unmeasured. Their framework, ThirstyFLOPS, quantifies both operational and embodied water for such systems.

The analysis folds in regional metrics for water use, power use, and the water intensity of local energy. Four famous machines serve as case studies: Marconi, Fugaku, Polaris, and Frontier. The authors compare water and carbon footprints side by side, exposing trade-offs between them. Regional water scarcity changes which machine looks greenest, they show. Nuclear-powered computing gets a careful hearing, with advantages and warnings both noted. The tool aims to ground future water-aware planning for computing infrastructure.
arxiv-2510-00671:
Nguyen and four co-authors introduce MILCO in this 2025 arXiv paper on multilingual information retrieval. Learned sparse retrieval represents queries and documents as weighted word lists, which is fast and transparent, but it has mostly worked in English alone. MILCO maps text from many languages into one shared English lexical space through a multilingual connector. A two-stage training recipe aligns those sparse representations first, then applies contrastive training to sharpen retrieval quality.

Rare names and entities can vanish when projected into English, so a LexEcho head adds a source-language view through a special echo token. On standard multilingual and cross-lingual benchmarks, MILCO set state-of-the-art results among learned sparse systems and beat strong dense rivals such as BGE-M3. With aggressive pruning to about thirty active dimensions, the 560-million-parameter model still outperformed a similarly sized dense competitor using over a thousand.
arxiv-2510-00771:
Choi, Lee, Lim, and Kang at Yonsei University present UniverSR in this 2025 arXiv paper on audio super-resolution. The task rebuilds full, clear 48 kilohertz audio from low-rate recordings that miss high frequencies and sound muffled. Most generative systems work in two stages, predicting a mel-spectrogram and then calling a separate neural vocoder to make the waveform. That vocoder caps the final quality no matter how good the first stage gets.

UniverSR removes the vocoder entirely and learns the distribution of complex spectral coefficients with flow matching. An inverse Fourier transform then turns those coefficients straight into a waveform. Trained on a large mixed collection of speech, music, and environmental sound, the model handled upsampling from 8, 12, 16, and 24 kilohertz inputs. Objective and listening tests placed it at state-of-the-art level across those settings.
arxiv-2510-01471:
Xiang, Xu, and Lu turn a fine-tuned language model into the surrogate brain of Bayesian optimization for costly, high-dimensional design problems. Gaussian processes crumble when inputs turn discrete or the dimension climbs. Language models, by contrast, digest odd-shaped inputs with ease.

Only the last layer carries Bayesian uncertainty, handled with a variational fit. Low-rank adapters fine-tune the big model cheaply alongside that posterior. Recursive updates between rounds keep it current without retraining from scratch. An ensemble of adapters with data-adaptive weights removes the need to hand-pick setups. Drug discovery and materials design headline the costly uses. Exploration and caution stay in balance through the model's own spread. Parallel recursive updates make the ensemble scalable in practice. Odd-shaped inputs stop being second-class citizens in optimization. Sample thrift is the currency costly trials pay in. A linear head keeps uncertainty honest.
arxiv-2510-01571:
Cao and co-authors ask what reinforcement learning actually teaches a protein language model beyond its pre-training. Such models learn protein patterns from huge sequence collections, then designers fine-tune them for useful molecules. Whether reward-driven training uncovers genuinely new sequence logic, or just samples favorites faster, stayed unclear.

The team compared two model families, three learning algorithms, and four experimental testbeds. Rewards did steer sampling toward high-value regions more efficiently. Diversity shrank as a side effect, and outputs contracted toward safe, familiar territory. The study maps both the reach and the price of exploration in protein design. Shrinkage was measured directly, giving the contraction a number rather than a vibe. Reward design decides which trade-off a project actually buys. Pre-training still supplies the raw vocabulary of sequences. Designers chasing novelty may need diversity guards alongside rewards. Exploration, it turns out, exploits too.
arxiv-2510-01771:
Shi, Abdulah, Sun, and Genton build a federated modeling framework for spatial data in this 2025 statistics paper. Sensor networks and other spatial data sources often cannot share raw data, due to privacy and bandwidth limits. Federated modeling trains one global model while data stay in place. Older federated methods either ignored spatial dependence or waited on slow participants.

Their framework is asynchronous, so fast nodes never wait for stragglers. It rests on low-rank Gaussian process approximations that capture spatial correlation cheaply. Block-wise optimization, gradient correction, and adaptive aggregation keep the updates stable despite delays. The authors prove linear convergence with an explicit term for update staleness. Experiments matched synchronous methods when resources were balanced across nodes. Under uneven, heterogeneous conditions the asynchronous method won clearly, which suits real sensor networks.
arxiv-2510-01871:
Villemaud, Sankagiri, and Grossglauser price the hidden thresholds behind coarse ratings in this 2025 paper. Recommenders collect stars and likes, then try to recover a fine ranking of items. Their model gives each item a true score and each user a personal threshold. A user rates an item positively only when its score clears that user's bar.

Everyone agrees on the true item order, yet reconstructing it is surprisingly expensive. Any method sorts items into ordered bins with ties inside each bin. The authors prove that a near-perfect ranking, measured by Spearman distance, needs on the order of n squared users. Comparisons would need only n log n queries for the same job. The gap pays for hunting down users whose thresholds sit in the right places. A matching algorithm reaches the bound up to a log factor. Threshold diversity is thus both necessary and costly.
arxiv-2510-02171:
Dervakos and four co-authors let a performer's body steer audio effects in real time in this 2025 paper. Music performance is bound up with expressing emotion, something machines cannot feel. Their system, witheFlow, aims at collaboration rather than automation. It reads features from both biosignals and the live audio, then modulates effects accordingly.

The design is deliberately lightweight, running locally on a laptop. It is open source and needs only a compatible audio workstation plus sensors. The authors present it as a proof of concept, an instrument for exploring human-machine performance. Effects follow the performer's state without breaking the flow of playing. That responsiveness turns physiological signals into a new expressive channel. The paper contributes a working prototype and a design stance: keep the human as the emotional source. Studios and stages get a tool for performances that breathe with the player.
arxiv-2510-02271:
Du and co-authors built InfoMosaic-Bench, a test for agents that must gather facts from many sources. Their 2025 machine learning paper looks beyond plain web search. Web pages are noisy, and many tasks need exact domain knowledge. New tool protocols now let agents query specialized services directly. The benchmark spans six areas, including medicine, finance, maps, and video. Tasks were made with a pipeline called InfoMosaic-Flow. Each task forces the agent to mix search with domain tools.

The authors ran current agents on the benchmark and studied their failures. Agents often showed confirmation bias, trusting early guesses over tool output. They also guessed beyond the evidence and misread task intent. Clear domain clustering in the task set confirmed the coverage was broad. The benchmark gives builders a shared yardstick. It shows that tool access alone does not guarantee careful research.
arxiv-2510-02471:
Barber and Pananjady explain why a popular forecast interval method works on time series data. Their 2025 statistics paper studies split conformal prediction. The method wraps honest error bands around any forecast. Its guarantees assume data points can swap places freely. Time series break that assumption through memory and drift. Forecasters with memory make the violation worse. Yet the method performs strongly in practice anyway. The authors measure exactly how much coverage is lost. A new quantity, the switch coefficient, captures the damage. It gauges how strongly time dependence breaks the swapping property.

Their bounds tie coverage loss directly to that coefficient. Mild dependence therefore costs only mild accuracy. Predictors that remember the past fit the same framework. Weather, energy, and finance forecasts all lean on such bands. Users gain a reason to trust the intervals. Theory finally matches a widespread empirical habit.
arxiv-2510-02571:
Mei, Shorinwa, and Majumdar give video generation models a way to say how unsure they are. Their 2025 paper is the first on uncertainty for video models. Video generators hallucinate plausible but false footage. Users get no signal about which outputs to trust. The authors build a full framework for that missing signal. A calibration metric uses robust rank correlation without strict assumptions. Their method, S-QUBED, works as a black box on any generator. Latent modeling splits uncertainty into two named parts. One part reflects data randomness, the other model ignorance.

A benchmark dataset supports fair comparison of methods. Experiments showed the method stays well calibrated. The two uncertainty parts separated cleanly in practice. Sampling several videos is the main extra cost. Safety critical uses need exactly this kind of honesty. A generator that knows its limits can flag risky outputs. Video AI takes a step toward accountable deployment.
arxiv-2510-02671:
Bakman and co-authors measure how unsure a language model should be when answering from supplied context. Their 2025 machine learning paper tackles contextual question answering. Uncertainty research has mostly covered closed book factual questions. Real systems answer from documents, where doubt works differently. The team defines a token level measure of total uncertainty. Splitting that measure isolates the part due to model ignorance. An idealized, perfectly prompted model stands in for the truth. The gap becomes hidden state differences between the two models. Three features approximate that gap in practice.

Context reliance, comprehension, and honesty carry the signal. A handful of labeled samples tuned the estimator. It beat popular baselines on the contextual tests. Knowing when a model guesses protects downstream users. Retrieval systems can flag answers for human review. The theory ties doubt to readable internal features. Future work hunts for more such features automatically.
arxiv-2510-02771:
Macinic and Valles find obstructions for conic and line arrangements whose Chern polynomial splits. Their 2025 mathematics paper works in algebraic geometry. The objects are lines and conics in the complex plane. A bundle of special vector fields attaches to each curve. Its Chern polynomial may factor neatly over the integers. The authors show that splitting forces structural restrictions. Their results merge two earlier lines of work. One covered line setups whose polynomials split. The other covered free curves and their constraints. A new splitting test uses restrictions to smooth conics.

Addition and deletion arguments drive the proofs. Rank two bundles get tested curve by curve. Obstructions turn a numeric coincidence into geometry. Freeness questions sit at the center of arrangement theory. Split polynomials are rare enough to demand explanation. Tests like these prune the search for examples. The paper sharpens tools for classifying singular curves.
arxiv-2510-02871:
Bartlett-Tisdall, Ge, and Herzog ask a sharp theory question. Can a line defect interact inside a free quantum field theory? Conformal defects keep scale symmetry along with shape symmetry. Free bulk fields seem too plain to host rich defect behavior. The authors argue that such defects can exist after all. The key is to break inversion symmetry, a flip of space.

They point to a special ratio in three-point functions. The ratio respects the conformal group in full. Under inversion alone, though, it flips its sign. That sign gives the defect room to interact. A toy model makes the claim concrete. A free scalar field fills the bulk space. Fermions live only on the line itself. A Yukawa term couples the scalar to those fermions. Free light theory and free bulk fermions may host them too. The result widens the map of defect theories.
arxiv-2510-03271:
Liang and co-authors make the decision boundary of a language model drawable for the first time. A decision boundary separates inputs a model classifies differently. For language models, huge vocabularies make it seem unbuildable. Sequence space explodes while generation runs autoregressively. Their Decision Potential Surface reframes the problem through confidence. The surface measures how strongly sampled sequences favor each class. Its zero-height contour is the decision boundary exactly.

A practical algorithm approximates that surface with finite sampling. K-DPS needs only K rounds of sequence sampling per input. Error bounds cover absolute, expected, and concentrated error. More sampling trades directly against those errors. Experiments across models and corpora validated the construction. Enclosed regions of the surface form the decision regions. Interpretability gains a geometric tool it lacked for language models. Security and robustness analysis can use the same maps. Knowing where a model flips is basic self-knowledge.
arxiv-2510-03371:
Nedelkoski and colleagues present a 2025 arXiv paper on training large models across machines linked by slow networks. Top data centers enjoy fast cables, but pooled spare computers often do not. Their method syncs model copies rarely and shrinks what each sync must send. The trick treats the optimizer's momentum as a signal and splits it into fast and slow parts. Only the fast changing parts travel between machines at each sync round.

Tests cut communication by up to sixteen times compared with the DiLoCo baseline method. The gains held across transformer language models and image networks alike. Because each node trains locally for long stretches, weak links hurt far less. Groups without a flagship data center could still train serious models together. Universities, hospitals, and firms in different cities are natural users. The work widens who gets to build large models, not just who can rent the biggest clusters.
arxiv-2510-03471:
Zhang and colleagues present a 2025 arXiv paper introducing a shared testbed for quadcopter control under stress. Adaptive controllers promise to keep drones steady through wind, shifting loads, and failing rotors. Yet each research group tests on its own simulator and tasks, so results rarely compare cleanly. Their suite, built on the RotorPy simulator, standardizes disturbances, flight paths, and scoring. A library of adaptive and plain controllers ships with the testbed for instant comparison.

Users can dial in gusts, payload shifts, rotor faults, and control delays in repeatable mixes. Automated stress testing sweeps many conditions without hand holding. Metrics track both path accuracy and robustness across the runs. The authors show the suite handling many scenario and trajectory types with one setup. Shared ground like this should speed honest progress in drone control, a field where real world crashes make simulation discipline essential.
arxiv-2510-03571:
Karabulut, Manna, and Develder present a 2025 arXiv paper benchmarking graph neural networks that detect faults in power distribution grids. Grids keep changing shape as switches flip, gear fails, and rooftop solar joins, so detectors must generalize beyond their training layout. The study pairs recurrent networks for time patterns with several graph networks for spatial structure. It is the first to try GraphSAGE and attention based graph models in this pipeline for fault diagnosis, the authors say.

On the IEEE 123 node test network, one attention variant, RGATv2, generalized when sensor counts changed after training. Its score fell by only about twelve percent. Pure recurrent models collapsed, with scores dropping by up to about sixty percent. Other graph variants lost up to about a quarter of their score. Grid operators need detectors that survive the reshaping of real networks, and attention based graph models now lead that race.
arxiv-2510-03771:
Handa and colleagues present a 2025 arXiv paper optimizing how online stores rewrite shopper queries, using simulated customers as the judge. A rewritten query should capture what the shopper wants, but there is no correct answer to grade against. Their framework, OptAgent, fields language model agents that role play customers with reasoning styles. The agents' average score becomes the fitness signal for a genetic algorithm that breeds rewrites. One thousand queries across five categories supplied the test bed.

Rewrites improved by twenty two percent over the shoppers' original queries. They beat a model rewriting baseline by three percent. Gains were largest on long tail queries where intent is hard to read. Reward models freeze one judge's taste; a panel of simulated shoppers stays closer to preference diversity. The blueprint generalizes to other subjective tasks where answers do not exist, from support replies to product descriptions.
arxiv-2510-03871:
Filatov and colleagues wrote this 2025 arXiv paper searching for one rule behind good training settings for language models. As models and datasets grow, the best learning rate and batch size shift unpredictably. Earlier methods transfer settings across model size or dataset size, but not both together. Using the Scion optimizer, the team hunted for a shared pattern across thousands of runs.

They found that every optimal setting shared the same operator norm in the model's output layer. They call this pattern norm transfer. Holding that norm fixed is necessary for top performance, though not by itself sufficient. The team also measured how the best learning rate and batch size scale with dataset size, matching Adam's rules. Tuning separate rates per layer group helped too, with the output layer most sensitive. They released code and logs from over two thousand runs for others.
arxiv-2510-03971:
Prakash and Buvanesh wrote this 2025 arXiv paper on a training failure that hits language models on hard tasks. Reinforcement learning improves models when they sometimes sample a correct answer. If the base model never solves a task, every reward is zero and learning stalls completely. The authors study this zero-reward barrier on a controlled graph search task.

They reimplemented several recent fixes: dense rewards, diversity incentives, and better credit assignment. None of these methods crossed the barrier when the base model never produced a correct answer. A simple data change worked instead: adding easier training examples gave the model a foothold. From those wins, the model bootstrapped its way to solving the original hard task. No change to the learning algorithm itself was needed. The authors urge evaluations to include tasks where models start from total failure. They released their baseline implementations for other researchers.
arxiv-2510-04171:
Naik and colleagues present this 2025 arXiv paper on choosing where a mobile robot should park before reaching for an object. A mobile manipulator must pick a base pose from which its arm can actually grasp the target. Classical planners and earlier learned policies assume precise object poses and environment models. This work instead plans from a top-down orthographic projection of the scene, which needs no such privileged state.

Their system, VBM-Net, first uses an equivariant TransporterNet that exploits spatial symmetries to propose candidate base poses. Reinforcement learning picks the best candidate from that graph. In tests, VBM-Net matched classical planners' solution quality with much less computation time. A policy trained purely in simulation transferred successfully to a real robot. Vision-only base placement removes a brittle dependency on perfect scene knowledge, a step toward dependable household and warehouse robots.
arxiv-2510-04271:
Tan and colleagues present this 2025 arXiv paper on improving shared scooter and bike systems by adding a few vehicles that can rebalance themselves. Shared micromobility fleets drift out of balance as riders cluster vehicles where demand has already passed. Conventional scheduling redistributes vehicles only once or twice daily, so atypical demand patterns quickly overwhelm it. Autonomous shared vehicles could move continuously toward emerging demand, but operators need a policy for deploying and steering them.

The proposed framework, SMART, uses hierarchical reinforcement learning to coordinate both decisions. A high-level policy chooses where autonomous vehicles start service. A low-level policy rebalances them in real time as demand changes. Experiments with real Chicago e-scooter data showed the framework improving all three conventional scheduling baselines. Demand satisfaction rose by more than seven percent in the weakest reported comparison, while the method retained strong generalization.
arxiv-2510-04371:
Naimeng Ye and five coauthors wrote this 2025 paper on making AI agents work faster. Agents often act one step at a time, and each step needs a slow call to a model or a tool. A chess game between two top agents can take hours for this reason. The authors borrow a chip design trick and guess the next action early, so steps can run side by side.

The system pairs a fast guessing model with a slower, trusted actor model. When a guess matches the real action, time is saved and nothing is lost. Tests covered games, online shopping, and web search, plus a looser version for operating system tasks. The guesses matched the real next action up to 55 percent of the time in the tests. That match rate cut waiting time by a large share. Stronger guessing models and guessing several steps ahead helped even more.
arxiv-2510-04671:
Chao Liu and six coauthors wrote this 2025 paper on cleaning up the questions patients ask online. People describe symptoms in rambling posts full of side details and lay words. Doctors answer faster when the question is short and lands on its real focus. Their framework, FocusMed, trains language models to summarize such questions while keeping that focus. Direct fine tuning, they found, drifts from the true focus and invents details.

FocusMed first prompts the model to pull the core focus straight from the original wording. It then fine tunes on data that pairs each rambling question with its focused summary. A scoring step checks candidate summaries on several quality axes and keeps the best. On two standard data sets, the framework beat prior methods on every metric they used. It also cut hallucinated content, which matters when summaries guide care. The team released the code for others to build on.
arxiv-2510-04771:
Damien Korber and a team of coauthors wrote this 2025 astronomy paper on the faintest galaxies of the early universe. They used the GLIMPSE survey with the Webb telescope, through a lensing galaxy cluster. The cluster magnifies background galaxies from the young universe. The team measured hydrogen and oxygen emission from a sample of galaxies. From those fluxes they built the luminosity function, a census by brightness.

The faint end of that census rises less steeply than the ultraviolet census at the same era. Fewer dim emitting galaxies appear than a scaling would predict. The team weighs explanations: bursty star formation, falling metal content, or a turn down in the ultraviolet census. Falling metals plus bursty histories together can reconcile the two counts. They convert the census into the rate of ionizing photons those galaxies supply. Mid brightness galaxies supply a share of that budget. The faintest ones contribute almost nothing.
arxiv-2510-04971:
Uroš Šmajdek and Ciril Bohak of the University of Ljubljana present a tool for exploring names in large text collections in this 2025 arXiv paper. Corpora mention people, places, and organizations thousands of times. The same entity can appear under many spellings and contexts. Plain keyword search cannot show how those mentions connect.

Their system, NERVIS, draws the collection as an interactive graph. Nodes stand for documents, single mentions, and merged entities. Users can filter the graph, follow clusters of related mentions, and fix wrong links by hand. An expert in digital humanities tested the tool on historical print media. She judged the prototype ready for real research use.
arxiv-2510-05371:
Lorenzo Riva and Martina Rovelli build an explicit combinatorial model for freely adding adjoints in this 2025 arXiv paper. In higher category theory, a morphism has adjoints when certain unit and counit maps satisfy the snake equations. Freely adjoining right adjoints to every morphism of an infinity-category is a key universal construction. It also underlies the cobordism hypothesis in topology.

Their model, built from zigzags, realizes this free adjunction concretely. They prove the construction is universal: any other way of adding adjoints factors through it. A geometric analogue connects the combinatorics to the walking adjunction picture. Iterating the construction adds right adjoints dimension by dimension. The paper closes with speculative observations about higher-dimensional behavior and a possible broader universal property.
arxiv-2510-05471:
Everaert and colleagues improve a diamond-based tool for measuring magnetic responses. Nitrogen-vacancy centers in diamond can sense tiny magnetic fields with sharp spatial detail. Such sensors help study new magnets, test metals for hidden flaws, and guide heat-based cancer treatments. The sensors normally fail when the driving field grows strong, which blocks many uses.

The team adds a phase tuning trick, called SIPHT, to the standard sensing routine. The trick cancels the distortion that a strong drive field causes in the sensor. In lab tests, the new method kept its signal where the standard method faded. The team also detected eddy currents in copper, aluminum, and titanium samples. The timing delays in those signals matched each metal's conductivity, as theory expects. The advance opens strong-field measurements that diamond sensors could not reach before. That reach matters for medical and industrial testing alike.
arxiv-2510-05571:
Liu and colleagues build agents that turn research papers into polished presentations. Good promotion now matters for a paper's reach, yet automated tools make bland slides. Their systems suffer weak storytelling, plain design, and no way to fix themselves. Their 2025 framework, EvoPresent, attacks all three flaws with a self-improvement loop.

A model called PresAesth scores slide beauty and flags design defects. Agents draft slides, take that feedback, and refine their work in rounds. Virtual presenters then deliver the result with scripts and video. The team also built a benchmark from 650 conference papers and 2,000 slide pairs. Tests show feedback quality, not starting skill, drives real self-correction. Multi-task training gave the beauty model stronger general skill than single-task training. Pipelines also trade visual design against content depth. The loop reaches high quality in fewer rounds than rivals.
arxiv-2510-05671:
Kumar and colleagues build artificial synapses from a new memory device. Deep networks shuttle weights to off-chip memory, wasting energy and time. ULTRA RAM promises high endurance, extreme retention, and tiny switching energy. Their 2025 paper wires it into a synaptic array for on-chip learning.

A physics-based compact model captures charge trapping in the device's floating gate. Circuit simulations then benchmark a full synaptic core with CMOS peripherals. The design trains and runs a neural network entirely on chip. Against a CMOS baseline, area improves by about one point eight times. Energy improves by about one point five times at ninety-one percent training accuracy. The device endures over ten million program-erase cycles in testing. Retention is rated beyond a thousand years, far past deployment needs. Projections at advanced nodes beat SRAM and several rival memories.
arxiv-2510-05871:
Stoisser and colleagues create reasoning training data for biology without any labels. Synthetic chain-of-thought traces train large reasoning models with step-level supervision. Filtering those traces normally needs ground-truth labels from expensive wet-lab experiments. Their 2025 method filters by the model's own uncertainty instead.

Multiple traces are sampled per example, then scored for confidence. Self-consistency across samples and predictive perplexity quantify that confidence. Only the lowest-uncertainty traces survive into the training set. A hybrid score combining both signals produces the most reliable traces. Per-class filtering matters because uncertainty scales differ across outcome classes. The task is cellular perturbation prediction for drug discovery and disease modeling. Fine-tuning on filtered data beats unfiltered data and strong reasoning baselines. Filtered accuracy also narrows the gap to ground-truth training substantially. Model-internal confidence becomes a substitute supervision signal for label-scarce domains.
arxiv-2510-06471:
Li, Ji, and Tiedemann test whether extra thinking time improves reasoning-model translation in a 2025 NLP paper. Test-time scaling boosts reasoning models on math and coding. Its value for translation was unknown. The study tests twelve reasoning models across diverse translation benchmarks.

Three setups structure the experiments: direct translation, forced longer reasoning, and post-editing. For general models translating directly, extra compute gave limited, uneven gains. Performance plateaued quickly. Domain-specific fine-tuning changed the picture outright. Fine-tuned models improved across the board to an optimal, self-determined reasoning depth. Forcing models past their natural stopping point always hurt quality. Post-editing told the opposite story. There, test-time scaling proved highly useful, making self-correction pay off. The upshot shifts inference-compute spending. Translation gains live in self-correction workflows and specialized models, not single-pass general generation.
arxiv-2510-06571:
Shumon Koga and Miroslav Krstic work on control theory for melting and freezing processes. Their 2025 paper studies the Stefan problem, a model where heat moves through a material while its boundary shifts. Think of ice melting, where the ice-water front moves over time. Here the boundary follows a higher-order response, which makes control harder.

The goal is a heat-flux control at the boundary that parks the moving front at a chosen point. The design must also respect safety limits on the material and the front. Koga and Krstic build the control with a method called PDE backstepping. They prove the limits hold by using the maximum principle for heat equations. A Lyapunov analysis then shows the closed system is globally stable, with errors decaying exponentially. Simulations confirm the front settles safely at its target. An outline extends the idea to third-order boundary motion.
arxiv-2510-06671:
Ahsan Cheema and Sunil Puria study a hidden form of hearing damage. Their 2025 paper concerns cochlear neural degeneration, which harms hearing without changing standard test results. People with this damage pass clinic tests yet struggle to follow speech. Finding test material that exposes the damage is the main challenge.

The authors use information theory to grade candidate speech tests. They model the ear with a computer simulation of hair cells and auditory nerve fibers. Fifty short words were tested under clean, sped-up, echoing, and combined conditions. Damage was varied by reducing how many nerve fibers of each type survive. Information loss grew steadily as damage increased. Time-compressed speech revealed the loss most strongly, while echo had a smaller effect. The findings identify fast, dense speech as the best probe for this hidden damage. Such probes could one day guide real clinical tests.
arxiv-2510-06771:
Chris Benson and six co-authors propose a quieter way to map the sky in millimeter light. Their 2025 paper combines two spectrometer designs for astronomy. Large mapping surveys need instruments that split light into many color channels. Existing designs suffer from high detector counts, losses, or hard fabrication limits.

Their hybrid pairs a Fourier transform spectrometer with an on-chip filterbank focal plane. The Fourier unit supplies medium resolution across a wide view. The superconducting filterbank then acts as a final disperser that slashes photon noise. The authors estimate noise falls by more than a factor of ten. That gain could enable surveys measuring carbon monoxide power spectra at strong signal levels. Their projections cite signal-to-noise ratios between ten and one hundred. Such surveys would need on the order of a million spectrometer hours. The design keeps the mapping speed that older post-dispersed systems sacrificed.
arxiv-2510-06871:
Huahui Yi leads a team making multimodal reasoning models safer without making them less helpful. Their 2025 paper names a risk they call the Reasoning Tax. Models that reason across images and text can talk themselves into unsafe answers. Most defenses filter only the final output, leaving the reasoning itself unconstrained.

Their framework, SaFeR-VLM, builds safety into the reasoning process through reinforcement learning. It trains on a curated set of ten thousand safety-critical cases. Unsafe trial answers get reflected on and corrected instead of discarded. A structured reward scores several dimensions and penalizes hallucinations and contradictions. The resulting seven-billion-parameter model beat GPT-5-mini on safety measures by several points. It beat Gemini-2.5-Flash by a wider margin still, near seventeen points. Helpfulness did not drop in their tests. The work argues that safety should shape how a model thinks, not just what it finally says.
arxiv-2510-07071:
Zheng Xing and Junting Chen build radio maps for antenna networks without knowing where the measurements came from. Their paper tackles channel state information, the data networks need to aim signals at users. Radio maps tie each location to its channel conditions. Building them normally requires location-labeled measurements, which real networks rarely provide.

Their approach works blind, using only channel data with no labels at all. A hidden Markov model links a user's path to how the channel evolves over time. Estimating that path unlocks construction of an angular power map. Theory adds a pair of results about location accuracy limits. With base stations scattered, the error bound can vanish at any signal quality. With stations confined to a small region, some error survives even endless measurements. On network data, their method located users within eighteen meters on average. Most measurements came from a single serving cell.
arxiv-2510-07471:
Li and Zhang simulate chains of quantum repeaters, the relay stations a future quantum internet needs. Their 2025 paper tackles entanglement distribution over hundreds of kilometers. Direct generation protocols fail exponentially with distance. Repeaters split the journey into segments, then swap and purify entanglement across them. The framework models heralded link generation, Bell-state swapping, and multi-round purification under continuous depolarizing noise. Chain length, noise level, and purification depth are all configurable, letting designers explore the trade-off space before anyone builds hardware for a given route.

Memory decoherence emerges as the binding constraint: stored entanglement rots while waiting for neighboring links. Purification claws back fidelity at the price of time and extra pairs. Generation time and purification cost grow rapidly as noise rises. The authors present the tool as a deliberately simplified testbed, not a full network simulator.
arxiv-2510-07571:
Baranau asks a mischievous question with a serious answer: what is the fastest possible diffusion? The 2025 paper discards the trivial cheat of teleporting a spike into uniformity instantly. Instead it defines the optimum locally in time. At each instant, the process must maximize the differential entropy of the probability density, subject to a fixed rate of change measured by Kullback-Leibler divergence from the current state. That variational problem yields an explicit evolution equation.

The author exhibits special solutions and a numerical example. In the example, the optimal process spreads dramatically faster than classical diffusion under the same budget of change. The work is exploratory, opening questions about the equation's solution types rather than closing them.
arxiv-2510-08171:
Sardinero, Cayao, Seoane Souto, and Burset wrote this 2025 paper on exotic pairing in Josephson junctions threaded by magnetic textures. Such junctions are a controllable route to topological superconductivity and Majorana bound states. Using a tight-binding Green function method, the authors computed the pairing induced at the junction under varied conditions. In the ordinary regime, even-frequency singlet pairing dominates. The topological regime looks different.

There, Majorana states appear at the interface edges with robust odd-frequency triplet pairing. When the Majorana states are decoupled, that pairing shows a sharp divergent peak at zero frequency, tied to their self-conjugate nature. Coupling the states turns the peak into shifted resonances. A nonmagnetic break creates extra inner Majorana modes, while the outer modes keep their character. The results promote odd-frequency triplet pairing as a practical fingerprint of topological superconductivity.
arxiv-2510-08471:
Andreas Bluhm, Marius Lemm, Tim Möbus, and Oliver Siebert learn external potentials for fermions in continuous space in a 2025 arXiv paper. Knowing the potential acting on a quantum system lets physicists work out its behavior. Coulomb potentials, from electric charges, are the key case for chemistry. Continuous space is harder than lattice models: the state space is infinite-dimensional.

The Laplacian operator, which sets kinetic energy, is unbounded in the continuum, so information can spread without a speed cap. Their modular algorithm mixes new optimization methods with information-propagation bounds. Prior regularity assumptions on the potential keep the problem controlled. The result covers Coulomb interactions in any dimension plus other physical potential classes. One application is locating nuclei and ions and measuring their charges in quantum chemistry. The authors frame it as a foundation for a scalable fermion toolkit.
arxiv-2510-08771:
Li and a team of co-authors bring a faster attention method to image super-resolution in this 2025 arXiv paper. Super-resolution means rebuilding a sharp, detailed picture from a small or blurry one. The standard attention step compares every part of an image with every other part, so its cost grows steeply with image size. A leaner form, linear attention, grows only in step with size, but it had resisted use in realistic photo enhancement.

Their system, LinearSR, fixes three linked problems. A fine-tuning plan keyed to an early warning point in training stops the model from diverging. A team of specialist sub-networks, routed by signal quality, balances sharp looks against faithful detail. Lightweight guidance then steers the result without heavy extra cost. The finished model matches the best perceptual quality in the field while its core step runs at top speed.
arxiv-2510-09271:
Schemitt and co-authors benchmark quantum-proof digital signatures inside blockchain conditions, finding the feared slowdown is smaller than expected, in this 2025 arXiv paper. Blockchains rely on signatures to prove who authorized each transaction, and the standard scheme, ECDSA, would fall to a large quantum computer. Post-quantum alternatives were standardized in 2024, but their cost inside real blockchains was largely unmeasured. The team proposes a benchmarking methodology and tests seven candidate schemes across five security levels.

They measured signing and verification times on varied hardware, then simulated the impact at blockchain scale. At the lowest security level, the new schemes added only minor overhead over ECDSA. At higher levels, some significantly outperformed the incumbent: one scheme verified a signature in a small fraction of ECDSA's time on an ARM laptop at level five. The implementation is released openly.
arxiv-2510-09371:
Nitish Panigrahy and seven co-authors, among them Don Towsley, propose a control framework for quantum networks in a 2025 arXiv paper. A future Quantum Internet must share entanglement, a fragile quantum link between distant nodes, among many applications at once. The authors allocate that resource in a fully decentralised way, guided by feedback rather than by one central planner.

Their framework, called QNUM, scores network performance by mapping both entanglement rate and quality into one optimisation goal. Their QPrimal-Dual algorithm reaches that goal using controllers that see only local state and exchange few classical messages. They prove the system settles to a stable state for well-behaved scoring functions, and they add schemes that cut overhead and guard against memory decay. In simulations of realistic networks, the method beat baseline strategies, scaled with size, and stayed robust to delay and decoherence.
arxiv-2510-09471:
Inés Altemir Mariñas, Anastasiia Kucherenko, Alexander Sternfeld, and Andrei Kucharavy describe a search engine for a language model's training data in a 2025 arXiv paper. What a model learns depends on its training text, yet even open models rarely let outsiders inspect that text at scale. The team built a full-text index over the training data of the Apertus model family.

Using Elasticsearch with parallel indices on the Alps supercluster, an energy-efficient machine built on arm64 chips, they indexed more than eight trillion tokens out of over fifteen trillion used in training. The work shows that a search tool from the web world can run on next-generation hardware and can index modern training corpora in full. The authors present the index as a safety tool, since harmful content can be searched directly, and as an offline curated search engine over the open web.
arxiv-2510-09571:
Khandakar Md Asif Elahi and five co-authors present a deep radio sky survey in a 2025 arXiv paper. Telescopes hunting the faint 21-centimetre signal from the Epoch of Reionisation, when the first stars lit up, need extremely precise calibration. That demands an accurate sky model of the field used for calibration, and arrays such as HERA rely on such reference models.

The team observed one HERA calibration field for twenty hours with the upgraded Giant Metrewave Radio Telescope in India. Their mosaic covers a square patch of sky at a frequency near one hundred forty-seven megahertz, reaching noise levels deeper than the existing GLEAM catalogue in the overlap region. They catalogue six hundred forty sources, about a quarter of them extended, with sub-arcsecond positions and fluxes consistent with other catalogues. Simulations suggest the new model changes predicted visibilities by ten to twenty-five percent over the old one.
arxiv-2510-09871:
Nikeghbal, Amir Hossein Kargaran, and Jana Diesner probe hidden bias in large language models in this 2025 arXiv paper, which they call CoBia. Modern models pass standard safety checks more and more often, thanks to stronger guardrails. Yet in open conversation they can still slip into harmful views, such as racist claims.

The team uses constructed conversations, dialogues built to draw out views a model would not state under direct questioning. Their point is that bias can stay concealed in single test prompts and surface only across turns of talk. CoBia offers a way to test for that gap. The authors warn that passing a safety check does not prove a model is free of such views.
arxiv-2510-10071:
Zhang and co-authors present ADEPT in this 2025 arXiv paper on adapting language models to new domains. Continual pretraining updates a model on domain data, but it often causes catastrophic forgetting of general skill and gives the new domain too little capacity. Layer expansion adds trainable layers to hold the new knowledge.

ADEPT makes that expansion adaptive and decouples the tuning, so general and domain learning stop interfering. Uniform expansion, the authors argue, still entangles the two kinds of learning and weakens both. By expanding where the domain needs it and training the parts separately, the method aims to add expertise without erasing the base model. The trade-off between memory and mastery is the paper's central problem.
arxiv-2510-10171:
McFarlane derives toxicity bounds for liquidation incentives in this 2025 arXiv paper on decentralized finance. On-chain liquidations sell collateral through a constant-product automated market maker, a pricing rule used by decentralized exchanges. A liquidation incentive pays the liquidator a bonus, but slippage, the price loss on a large trade, changes the math.

McFarlane derives a slippage-aware condition for when a liquidation turns toxic, meaning value-destroying. For a fixed incentive, the familiar toxicity frontier tightens by a liquidity penalty factor. He derives that factor for the standard market maker and for a generalized form. The bounds help protocol designers set incentives that keep liquidations healthy instead of harmful.
arxiv-2510-10671:
Jinxuan Li and six co-authors survey a young field: reusing image and language foundation models for video tasks, in this 2025 arXiv paper. Training video language models from scratch is expensive in data and compute. Transfer learning from image models avoids much of that cost while matching or beating their performance. The authors present the first comprehensive review of this image-to-video transfer approach.

They first summarize the main foundation models and what each can do. They then sort existing techniques into two root families: methods that freeze the image features, and methods that adapt them, each with finer subcategories. The survey walks through applications from spatio-temporal video grounding to video question answering. The authors add their own experiments comparing paradigms across downstream tasks. They close with open challenges and promising directions, aiming to give the field a structured roadmap.
arxiv-2510-11371:
In ergodic theory, an extreme value law describes how rarely a moving system comes close to a target, and how the timing of those near misses is distributed. Jens Marklof, Andreas Strömbergsson, and Shucheng Yu extend such a law in this 2025 arXiv mathematics paper. Earlier work by Kirsebom and Mallahi-Karai covered horocycle flows on the space of two-dimensional lattices; this paper treats the simplest rank-k unipotent actions on spaces of higher-dimensional lattices.

The authors analyze hitting times and impact statistics relative to a shrinking surface of section, adapting a strategy Pollicott and Marklof used for hyperbolic surfaces. When the rank is maximal, the limit law comes from directional statistics of Euclidean lattices. For lower ranks, new distributions appear, and the authors derive precise asymptotics for their tails. The results connect the geometry of lattice spaces with statistics of rare close encounters.
arxiv-2510-11471:
Meta-learning, prompt tuning, in-context learning, and learned optimizers look different, but all reuse computation across tasks so systems adapt quickly. Sarthak Mittal, Divyat Mahajan, Guillaume Lajoie, and Mohammad Pezeshki argue these methods are one family in this 2025 arXiv machine learning paper. Their unified framework describes how the approaches differ mainly in which aspect of learning is amortized, initializations, update rules, or predictive mappings.

They sort models into parametric, implicit, and explicit regimes, depending on where task adaptation happens. They identify a scaling weakness: most methods process task data through a limited context, so they struggle with large datasets. Their answer is iterative amortized inference: models that refine a solution step by step over mini-batches, like stochastic optimization. The formulation bridges optimization-based meta-learning with the forward-pass adaptation of large language models, offering a scalable foundation for task adaptation.
arxiv-2510-11671:
Two clouds of ultracold atoms, linked by a radio wave field, can act like a magnet. Warm the clouds or change the link strength and that magnetic order can melt away. Sunilkumar V, Rajat, Gautam, and Roy chart this change in this 2025 arXiv condensed matter paper. They use Hartree-Fock-Bogoliubov theory in the Popov form to study the shift with and without heat.

For a uniform three dimensional cloud they map the two phases across heat and link strength. They trace the border between phases by watching a gap in the spin spectrum shrink toward zero. Magnetism fades as the cloud warms, showing the ordered phase giving way. In long thin traps, a spin breathing mode softens at the shift, and its low point moves to weaker links as heat grows. Pure heating, by contrast, stiffens every spin mode step by step.
arxiv-2510-12071:
Jin Hwa Lee, Matthew Smith, Maxwell Adam, and Jesse Hoogland argue that a training example's influence has a biography. Standard data attribution treats influence as a fixed number: this sample helped that prediction, period. But networks learn in stages, and the authors' 2025 arXiv paper builds a stagewise attribution framework grounded in singular learning theory.

Theory predicts influence should change non-monotonically, flipping sign and spiking at developmental transitions. A toy model confirms it, analytically and empirically: the flips map directly onto the model's progressive learning of a semantic hierarchy, coarse concepts first. The phenomena persist in large language models, where token-level influence shifts align with known developmental stages. A sample that teaches early structure may hinder late refinement, and static scores average that story away. For dataset curation and debugging, the timing of influence becomes as informative as its size.
arxiv-2510-12171:
Junkai Zhang and ten colleagues examine whether language models can actually reason about materials. MatSciBench, their 2025 arXiv benchmark, gathers thirteen hundred forty college-level problems spanning six primary fields and thirty-one sub-fields of materials science. Problems carry a three-tier difficulty rating based on the reasoning length required, detailed reference solutions for precise error analysis, and visual contexts for multimodal questions.

The verdict is humbling. Even the best model tested, Gemini two point five Pro, scores under eighty percent. Comparing reasoning strategies, self-correction, tool augmentation, and plain chain-of-thought, no single method wins across scenarios. Performance crumbles unevenly with difficulty, multimodal reasoning proves especially hard, and retrieval augmentation helps only selectively. Failure-mode analysis across models and methods rounds out the diagnosis. The benchmark's data and code are public.
arxiv-2510-12671:
Parent and Tanré settle a refined form of a classical conjecture about two ways of measuring a space's complexity, for rational spaces of any category, in a 2025 arXiv paper. The Lusternik Schnirelmann category counts how many contractible patches are needed to cover a space. The cone length counts the steps needed to build the space from suspensions. Category never exceeds cone length, and the two differ by at most one.

Lemaire and Sigrist conjectured in 1981 that the two are always equal for rational spaces. The conjecture held for category one and two, but Dupont refuted it in 1999 with a rational space of cone length four and category three. Parent and Tanré now provide, for every integer k above two, rational spaces with cone length one more than k and category exactly k. The gap Dupont found is therefore not an isolated case but occurs at every level.
arxiv-2510-12871:
Lithwick and colleagues settle a dispute about eccentric disks in this 2025 arXiv paper. Many disks around stars and planets are observed off-center, and theory disagreed on whether a pressureless disk held together by its own gravity can stay eccentric. The authors analyze small eccentric disturbances in such a disk.

They show an eccentric disk is possible only with a sharply truncated edge: the surface density must fall to zero at the edge and drop steeply where it vanishes. If either condition fails, the disturbance leaks into the thin edge region and never returns, killing the pattern. They confirm this three ways, through eigenvalue solutions, time evolution, and a new dispersion relation. As a byproduct they built a softening-free algorithm that models the disk far more accurately than standard methods.
arxiv-2510-12971:
Zhang and colleagues teach robots manipulation skills from ordinary human videos in this 2025 arXiv paper. Their system, Actron3D, needs only a few monocular, uncalibrated RGB videos per task, the kind anyone can record with a phone. Earlier video-based methods predicted movements in flat pixel space, which becomes ambiguous when lifted into real three-dimensional robot actions.

At the core sits a Neural Affordance Function, a compact object-centered representation. It distills geometry, appearance, and affordance, meaning what actions an object allows, from varied videos into a small neural network. That network acts as a skill memory. At deployment the system retrieves the relevant function and refines a precise six-degree-of-freedom policy through coarse-to-fine optimization. Across thirteen tasks in simulation and the real world, it beat prior methods by a wide margin in success rate using only two or three demonstrations each.
arxiv-2510-13071:
Fisher and Talet classify invariant measures for adic transformations in this 2025 arXiv mathematics paper. These act on path spaces of Bratteli diagrams, layered graphs that encode certain systems. Their measures, the distributions unchanged by the dynamics, were classified before only for locally finite cases. Earlier results covered fewer cases.

The authors develop a Frobenius normal form for reducible matrices, adapted to the nonstationary case. They add a matching notion of distinguished eigenvector and a nonstationary Frobenius-Victory theorem to complete the proof. They allow locally infinite ones. They give an exact condition for a measure finite on a subdiagram to become infinite on the full space. They also add a canonical cover that restores local finiteness. Results extend to adic towers. Examples include new models of the Integer Cantor Set transformation and nested circle rotations with finite or infinite total mass.
arxiv-2510-13271:
Gevers and Daelemans benchmark language models on a word-guessing board game in this 2025 arXiv paper. Abstract reasoning benchmarks often use grids or visual patterns far from the text these models train on. The game Concept, a verbal cousin of Pictionary where one player conveys a word through a fixed clue vocabulary, tests abductive reasoning, inferring the best explanation, in natural language instead.

Humans solve the game easily, succeeding over ninety percent of the time, but no state-of-the-art model exceeded forty percent success. The authors diagnose two weaknesses: models misread other players' strategic intent behind clue choices, and they fail to revise initial hypotheses as sequential clues arrive. Extending the evaluation beyond English, performance dropped further in Dutch, French, and Spanish, the lower-resource languages tested. The game thus exposes reasoning gaps that standard benchmarks hide.
arxiv-2510-13471:
Van Poppelen and Black-Schaffer study what periodic buckling does to twisted bilayer graphene. Their 2025 arXiv paper combines two known routes to flat electronic bands in graphene. Twisting two layers to a magic angle flattens bands and strengthens electron interactions. Buckling a single layer can also flatten bands, through spatially varying strain.

At large twist angles, mild buckling first flattens the bilayer bands beyond the monolayer case. Stronger buckling then widens the bands again instead. Two effects drive this reversal: interlayer coupling cuts in-plane kinetic energy, and a gap opens at the Dirac point. Buckling and twisting also compete, since one breaks sublattice symmetry and the other preserves it. That rivalry stops buckling from flattening bands further at the magic angle. Still, buckled samples beat pristine ones across a wide angle range.
arxiv-2510-13871:
Huaman and co-authors bring Quechua languages into Mozilla's Common Voice, spotlighting Puno Quechua as a case study. Their 2025 arXiv paper serves speech technology for under-resourced indigenous languages. Quechua varieties count millions of speakers yet lack the data modern voice tools demand. Community-driven collection offers a path that respects local ownership.

The paper surveys all seventeen Quechua languages now on the platform. Puno Quechua's onboarding is detailed step by step, from language setup to corpus gathering. Both read speech and spontaneous speech were collected for the variety. Common Voice now hosts 191.1 hours of Quechua speech overall, with most of it validated by listeners, the authors report. Puno Quechua contributes twelve hours of that total. A research agenda follows, covering technical hurdles and community engagement ethics. Indigenous data sovereignty anchors their recommendations for future collection.
arxiv-2510-13971:
Nathan L. Burwig and Damien A. Easson make the case for a closed universe, one whose space curves back on itself, in this 2025 arXiv paper. Cosmologists classify universes as flat, open, or closed depending on spatial curvature. Their new theorem concerns eternal universes that never hit a singularity, a point where physics breaks down.

They prove that flat and open expanding universes cannot be all three of nonsingular, geodesically complete, meaning paths extend forever. They also cannot stay consistent with the averaged null energy condition, a basic rule limiting negative energy. Any such complete flat or open universe must break that energy rule. Closed universes escape the trap: they admit complete, nonsingular solutions that respect the condition, with de Sitter space as the cleanest example. The authors also show positive curvature can mimic phantom dark energy, biasing reconstructions that assume flatness at about the one-percent level.
arxiv-2510-14071:
Puyu Yang, Vincent Traag, Rodrigo Costas, and Giovanni Colavizza study which papers get dragged into disputes on Wikipedia, and whether open access makes it more likely, in this 2025 arXiv paper. Wikipedia leans on scientific papers as trusted sources, and contested articles, where editors fight over content, reveal where knowledge debate gets heated.

Combining Wikipedia edit histories with metadata on the papers cited in the articles, the team finds disputes cluster in the social sciences and humanities, where topics carry social values and invite argument. Highly cited papers and papers in top journals are more likely to be disputed. Open access papers are far more likely to be caught up in disputes. They get contested sooner after they appear than paywalled ones. The authors trace the pattern to easier access speeding both engagement and scrutiny. The link between openness and disputes varies by field, matching editorial cultures across Wikipedia.
arxiv-2510-14271:
Yilun Zheng and co-authors argue that less is more for the knowledge graphs used in retrieval-augmented generation, in this 2025 arXiv paper. Graph-based systems feed language models structured facts. But the graphs are usually built by language models themselves. They come out noisy, full of duplicate entities and shaky relationships, which degrades answers and inflates cost.

Their framework, DEG-RAG, denoises the graph in two ways: entity resolution merges redundant entities that refer to the same thing, and triple reflection examines each subject-predicate-object fact and removes wrong relations. The result is a more compact, higher-quality graph. The authors evaluate the denoised graphs against their unprocessed counterparts and report better retrieval and generation performance, alongside an evaluation of entity resolution methods for language-model-generated graphs. The work treats graph cleaning as a first-class step rather than an afterthought in building retrieval systems.
arxiv-2510-14871:
Wang and a large team of co-authors introduce, in a 2025 arXiv paper, a compiler stack that maps artificial intelligence workloads onto AMD's neural processing units. Spatial chips like these gain their speed from fine-grained control: where data sits, what runs where, and in what order. General-purpose compilers hide exactly those details, wasting the hardware. The authors argue compiler infrastructure must expose orchestration, not abstract it away.

Their open-source stack, MLIR-AIR, adds a dialect that represents asynchronous, hierarchical operations across compute and memory resources. With it, the compiler schedules work spatially, spreads it across hardware regions, and overlaps communication with computation, without hand-written scheduling or runtime improvisation. Two case studies show the payoff: matrix multiplication and the attention block of the LLaMA 2 model. Matrix multiplication reached up to 78.7 percent compute efficiency in the reported runs, nearly matching state-of-the-art hand-optimized code.
arxiv-2510-15271:
Jingrui Yu and seven colleagues at NVIDIA speed up structure-from-motion, the technique that rebuilds 3D scenes and camera paths from overlapping photos. Their 2025 arXiv paper presents cuSfM, a system that runs the heavy computation on graphics processors using CUDA, NVIDIA's parallel computing platform. Fast, accurate camera poses are the base requirement for mapping in self-driving, robotics, and virtual simulation.

Because the system works offline, it can spend computing power freely to favor accuracy over speed of response. GPU parallelism lets it use demanding but precise feature extractors and build complete, non-redundant links between images. It also supports map-based localization and the fine-tuning of camera alignment between sensors. In tests across varied scenarios, cuSfM beat the widely used COLMAP system on both accuracy and processing speed while keeping global consistency. The team released it as an open-source Python package, PyCuSfM.
arxiv-2510-15471:
Vu Tram Anh Khuong leads a second team paper on micro-expression recognition, this time improving the motion features themselves. Their 2025 arXiv paper notes that most optical flow methods, which track pixel movement between frames, use only the rising phase of an expression, from onset to peak. The falling phase, from peak back to rest, carries key timing information that those methods throw away.

Their combined optical flow merges both phases into one feature representation. The rising phase shows how a muscle engages, while the falling phase shows how it releases, and the pair gives a fuller picture of the expression's dynamics. On two standard benchmark datasets, CASME II and SAMM, the combined features beat methods built on a single optical flow. The authors present the gain as evidence that the neglected second half of each micro-expression holds real signal.
arxiv-2510-15571:
Marcin Hajduk and five colleagues find signs of magnetic fields in the glowing shells that dying stars leave behind. Their 2025 arXiv paper studies planetary nebulae, the gas shells ejected by low- and mid-mass stars and then compressed by a fast stellar wind. Such shells normally emit thermal radio waves, and only two were known to show the non-thermal emission that betrays magnetic fields.

The team observed a sample of northern nebulae at a low radio frequency with the LOFAR array and added archival data at higher frequencies. In thirty nebulae the spectral slope fell below the thermal range, indicating non-thermal emission and thus magnetic fields. Most of those were bipolar nebulae, which are linked to binary central stars, and most were fairly large. The authors suggest magnetic fields may be common in smaller nebulae too, but hidden under stronger thermal glow.
arxiv-2510-15671:
Quantum Hall transitions are famous for universal critical behavior, yet experiments and theory still disagree on exponents. Qiwei Wan and Yi Zhang ask whether sample thickness explains part of the mismatch, in a 2025 arXiv paper. They study layered Weyl semimetals with disorder and a magnetic field, varying the thickness of the slab. Recursive methods track localization lengths and the local density of states across the transition. Thin samples should behave two-dimensionally, while thick ones approach three dimensions.

They find finite thickness pulls scaling away from pure two-dimensional universality. As thickness grows, behavior crosses over toward the three-dimensional Gaussian unitary ensemble. The work warns that extra degrees of freedom like thickness are often overlooked in critical phenomena.
arxiv-2511-00071:
Ertugrul Mutlu returns to wavelet-based parity finding as a testing of representation, not as a useful method, since parity is plainly read from the least significant bit. Integers up to ten thousand are encoded as fixed-width thirty-two-bit binary signals, split with a three-level Daubechies wavelet transform, summed up by coefficient sizes, and grouped per subband without watching.

The study asks how a standard signal process preserves, boosts, or hides symbolic information hidden in a numeric representation, and how that extends. Machine learning readers get a guided probe of representation dependence. Parity's known answer makes it a clean instrument for gauging what a process does to information.
arxiv-2511-00171:
Rahul Ghosh, Baishali Chaudhury, and Hari Prasanna Das propose CompAgent, an agentic framework for checking whether images and media obey complex, evolving policy rules in media, entertainment, and advertising. Task-specific models need costly labeled data and generalize poorly, while general multimodal models have broad knowledge but miss fine visual details and structured rule application on their own.

An agent structure combines those strengths, decomposing compliance checks into steps that use tools and detailed inspection. Computer vision readers get the first agentic approach to this problem, as framed by the authors. Automated compliance could scale content review where rules change faster than datasets can be rebuilt.
arxiv-2511-00371:
Erfan Al-Hossami and Razvan Bunescu formalize a teaching method called Socratic debugging, where an instructor guides a student to find a bug alone instead of handing over the fix. Most beginner bugs grow from misconceptions, false beliefs about how a concept works. A guided reasoning path can lead the student to a program behavior that clashes with the false belief, and the clash prompts a lasting belief update.

The authors define the task of generating such reasoning trajectories and build a dataset of debugging problems annotated with them, some written by hand and some by language models. They then test model-based generators for both the trajectories and the Socratic dialogues built on them. A large judge-based evaluation found most generated trajectories correct and nearly all dialogue turns valid.
arxiv-2511-00471:
Jian Zhang, Chenglin Wang, and Shihui Zhu resolve two conjectures about solitons of the cubic-quintic nonlinear Schrödinger equation in three dimensions. The conjectures, posed by Killip, Oh, Pocovnicu, and Visan, concern how soliton properties vary monotonically: one with frequency, the other with mass. Settling them required fresh control over the variational structure behind these self-trapped waves.

Both conjectures are now completely resolved, and uniqueness of the energy minimizer is proved along the way. With those pieces in place, the authors establish sharp stability for the solitons, the strongest form of the stability statement. They also give the first classification of normalized solutions for the equation. The work closes a coordinated set of questions about how these waves behave and persist.
arxiv-2511-01071:
Fengxing Zhu studies sequence reconstruction over a deletion channel, a communication setting where symbols can vanish from a transmitted binary codeword. The record notes the main mistake in an earlier version has been corrected. The receiver sees several distinct outputs, each missing up to a fixed number of symbols, and wants to narrow the original message down to a short list of candidates.

Zhu determines the minimum number of channel outputs needed to guarantee such a list reconstruction. The key step is computing the largest possible intersection of several deletion balls, the sets of outputs that different candidate codewords could produce after deletions. Knowing that intersection size exactly pins down when the received outputs can still be consistent with too many candidates.
arxiv-2511-01371:
Sagar Dutta, Banani Basu, and Fazal Ahmed Talukdar detect faults in induction motors without touching the machine. Induction motors are the workhorses of industry, and catching their faults early matters. Their sensor is a wide angle antenna, whose reflection and transmission coefficients change with the motor's condition.

Spectrograms of those two signals carry distinct signatures for varied fault conditions. A deep neural network learns the patterns and the boundaries between classes. Using the reflection coefficient alone gave about ninety three percent correct calls, the transmission coefficient alone did better, and both combined reached perfect accuracy in their tests. The paper also checks how the antenna's working frequency, its spot, and the signal length affect the score.
arxiv-2511-01471:
Mikhail Belov and five colleagues argue that the flow of executed trades, rather than price itself, is the basic engine behind market movement. They define execution flow as the rate at which traded volume accumulates over time, and they present experiments on real market data meant to show it driving the dynamics.

To compute the flow they build a numerical framework based on the Radon-Nikodym derivative. The method automatically picks out thresholds that could serve as trading triggers, and it extracts a characteristic time scale from an eigenvalue problem. A second framework, built on the Christoffel function spectrum, is offered as an alternative to principal component analysis that survives a wider class of transformations of the input data.
arxiv-2511-01971:
William Pannell, William Ronayne, and Andreas Stergiou examine a structural question about the renormalisation group, the machinery that describes how a quantum field theory changes with energy scale. In favourable cases the flow is gradient-like, following the slope of a single function. The authors check this property to four-loop order in theories mixing scalar and fermion fields, in four dimensions and just below.

A modified beta function, the beta shift, turns out to be central, and they derive the conditions it must meet for gradient flow. Over a thousand such conditions emerge, all scheme-independent and satisfied whenever the needed results exist. They also show that, as the number of fields grows, conformal theories with a nonzero beta shift dominate the landscape.
arxiv-2511-02271:
Yucheng Song, Yifan Ge, Junhao Li, Zhining Liao, and Zhifang Liao proposed a framework for automatically writing radiology reports from medical images, but the authors withdrew the submission from arXiv. In their withdrawal notice they stated that problems with the training epochs and training strategy had caused numerical errors in the results comparison table. They had decided to withdraw the preprint because of those errors. Its reported performance figures should therefore not be relied on.

As submitted, the work had described a system called HTSC-CIF that split report generation into three levels: aligning medical entities with image locations, tightening text-image alignment through masked modelling. It also applied a causal intervention to remove spurious correlations between image and text. The authors presented experiments claiming it beat current methods, claims that the withdrawal leaves unestablished.
arxiv-2511-02371:
Rohan Wandre, Yash Gajewar, Namrata Patel, and Vivek Dhalkari design a retrieval system for AI agents that learn continuously from streams of text, images, video, and audio. Retrieval-augmented generation grounds a language model's answers in stored evidence. A lifelong stream creates two headaches: keeping the index fresh without costly rebuilding, and keeping the distinct modalities semantically aligned as embeddings drift apart.

Their architecture, LUMA-RAG, tiers its memory, spilling embeddings from a fast index into a compressed tier under strict memory budgets. A streaming alignment bridge keeps audio and image representations consistent through incremental updates, and a telemetry layer bounds alignment drift and quantisation error to give explicit safety guarantees on the top-ranked results. Experiments showed strong text-to-image retrieval, gentle degradation when memory was compressed, and provably stable audio-to-image rankings.
arxiv-2511-02571:
Tetiana Manzhos, Tetiana Ianevych, and Olga Melnyk work out what a popular ranking metric should score when a ranking is pure chance. Recommender and search systems are graded by mean average precision at a cutoff, which rewards relevant items placed near the top of a list. To judge whether a real system beats luck, evaluators need the chance baseline and, just as much, the size of the random wobble around it.

The authors derive formulas for both the expectation and the variance of average precision at a cutoff under random rankings. Two evaluation settings are covered, the offline model and the online model.
