The editors find no sign that weighty problems were discussed at the dinner, and the note serves to place the event in the conference record.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d371:
Charles Bohlen's minutes record a luncheon at Tehran on 30 November 1943, at half past one, where the three leaders took up Turkey and the Straits. Before the meal, Roosevelt read Stalin the Anglo-American staff recommendations, which he and Churchill had approved.

Stalin voiced great satisfaction and promised simultaneous Red Army offensives to match. On Turkey, the leaders agree on the invitation to President Inönü to meet them in Cairo. Churchill says he will offer the Turks only twenty squadrons of aircraft and some anti-aircraft regiments. He will offer no land forces. Hopkins warns that no Rhodes landing may be hinted at. The American side holds there are no landing craft for it. Talk then turns to Russia's wish for warm-water ports and an easier regime at the Dardanelles, which Churchill does not oppose in principle.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d471:
Britain's chiefs of staff answered in writing on December 3, 1943, with a memorandum of their own, printed in the State Department's Cairo-Tehran volume beside the American paper of the same date. The British chiefs had come to Cairo by way of Tehran, where the three leaders had met for the first time.

A written position let the British commanders state their case fully before the Combined Chiefs of Staff argued it out. The memorandum therefore captures London's military thinking at a hinge point of the war. Read against the American memorandum, it shows two allies who agreed on the enemy but still differed on where and how to strike him.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d571:
Joseph C. Grew, the Acting Secretary of State, wrote to the President on January 19, 1945. Grew, a career diplomat and former ambassador to Japan, was minding the department while Secretary Stettinius traveled. The message appears in the State Department's Cairo-Tehran volume.

January 1945 found Roosevelt about to leave for the Yalta Conference, and the department's business ran through Grew's steady hand. An acting secretary's letter to the President marks the flow of decisions continuing while principals traveled. For readers, the message shows the government at a changing of the guard: Hull gone, Stettinius new, and the next great summit only weeks away.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d71: A second Roosevelt letter to Churchill is dated October 29, 1943, and it is Document 71 of the Cairo and Tehran volume. Paired same-day letters from the president match the paired Churchill notes in the same run of papers, a measure of the season's pace. The catalog record names no subject for either. The printed text in the Foreign Relations series is the only guide to what each one carried.
frus-1944-quebec-d171: An editors' note in the Quebec volume records a meeting for which the only source is the President's Log. Churchill joined Roosevelt in the president's map room at the Citadel for a review of the latest war news. The discussion also covered naval problems in the Pacific and the difficulties of supply there. No fuller record of the conversation was found.
frus-1944-quebec-d271:
The Netherlands government sent this statement to Roosevelt through Schoenfeld on September 13, 1944, having no direct code link to Quebec. Foreign Minister van Kleffens asked that it be laid before the conference, since Pacific strategy was on the agenda. The Dutch argued that cutting Japan's communications with her occupied southern area would not by itself compel surrender there.

Japanese forces in Burma, Malaya, the Philippines, and the Indies had food and stocks enough to stay on, the statement warns, and might fight irregularly even after Japan's defeat. Delayed liberation would multiply suffering and doom prisoners and internees. The Dutch urged active liberation aimed first at the most valuable territory: Java, with its food, labor, roads, harbors, and airfields.
frus-1944-quebec-d71:
Under Secretary of State Edward R. Stettinius recorded this second memorandum on September 14, 1944, during the Quebec Conference. The memorandum appears in the State Department's Quebec 1944 volume, beside his opening-day paper.

Two Stettinius memoranda in three days show the department following the conference closely from Washington, where news of the Morgenthau Plan's acceptance caused immediate unease. The State Department had its own plans for Germany and for the peace organization. For readers, this paper records the home front of American diplomacy reacting, in real time, to a summit it had not attended.
frus-1945-50-intel-d171:
The title "Central Intelligence Group Directive No. 15" heads a text dated 1 October 1946. The Office of the Historian kept it as document 171 in the Foreign Relations intelligence volume for 1945 to 1950. The National Intelligence Authority, set up in January 1946, oversaw the Director of Central Intelligence and his Central Intelligence Group.

A directive is not advice: it is an order that offices below must follow until it is changed or replaced. For a reader, the gain is precision: this is the rule as the ruled were told to obey it. For a reader of the period, the piece fills one link in the chain between the war's end and the settled Cold War system.
frus-1945-50-intel-d271:
Director of Central Intelligence Hillenkoetter addressed a memorandum to the Executive Secretary of the National Security Council (Souers) on 5 May 1948. It stands as document 271 in the intelligence volume of Foreign Relations of the United States, covering 1945 to 1950. It was the CIA's first full year, and the Council was setting the rules for both open analysis and secret work.

A short memo could set a meeting, kill a plan, or start one. This one played its part in that daily traffic. The note's brevity hides its weight: men at this level did not write to each other for practice. For a reader of the period, the piece fills one link in the chain between the war's end and the settled Cold War system.
frus-1945-50-intel-d371:
"Central Intelligence Agency Memorandum of Comments on the Dulles Report" bears the date 28 February 1949. It survives in print as document 371 of the State Department's Foreign Relations volume on intelligence, 1945 to 1950. Three men — Dulles, Jackson, and Correa — were touring the CIA's work for the Council and taking notes for a report.

Reports were the heavy guns of paper work: slower than a memo, but built to end an argument. Senior men read the findings first and the detail as needed. The subject is spelled out in the title. The text gives the CIA's own comments on the Dulles Report, the outside survey of its first years.
frus-1945-50-intel-d71:
The presidential directive on the coordination of foreign intelligence activities, dated 22 January 1946, is the founding paper of the volume's second act. By it, Truman created the National Intelligence Authority and its working arm, the Central Intelligence Group. It is printed in Foreign Relations of the United States, in the retrospective volume on American intelligence from 1945 to 1950.

The directive made a board of the secretaries of State, War, and Navy, joined by the president's chief of staff. It set a director of central intelligence to serve them. It was a compromise: central in name, departmental in control, and far smaller than Donovan's dream. Yet from this seed grew the system that followed. Readers should read the directive whole: its few pages set terms that the rest of the volume argues over, clause by clause.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d171:
How much Soviet sway in Rumania would Washington accept? “Principal Rumanian Problems” calls that the fundamental question in this briefing book paper. Prepared for the President's trip, it is printed in the Malta and Yalta volume of Foreign Relations.

Under the armistice, the Allied Control Commission works under the general direction of the Soviet High Command. From Bucharest, prominent Rumanians have appealed straight to American officers for a sign of United States policy. The British fear that Soviet moves threaten Rumania's very life as a free state. The paper also charges that Soviet authorities settled some matters alone. Among them was the property of American-owned oil companies, though such questions belonged to all three governments together.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d271:
Green Hackworth, the State Department's legal adviser, sent the war crimes machinery forward on 22 January 1945. His covering note to the Secretary, printed in the Malta and Yalta volume, presents two memoranda marked A and B. One has already been signed at the top of the government.

Memorandum A, signed by the Secretary, Secretary Stimson, and the Attorney General, states the problem and suggests a course. Memorandum B casts the same ideas as a draft ready for signature, the first step toward setting the machinery in motion. A copy went to Judge Rosenman. The plan rests on a short-lived international tribunal to try the principal culprits. Lesser offenders would face occupation courts and the national courts of the wronged countries.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d371:
First place in the queue for German reparations goes to those who bore the main burden of the war. So opens the Soviet proposal of February 7, 1945, laying down basic principles for exacting reparations from Germany. Other countries would receive payment only in the second place. The question of German labor as payment was set aside for later debate.

Payment in kind would come in two set forms. The first was removal, in a single payment at the war's end, from Germany's national wealth at home and abroad. Equipment, machine tools, ships, rolling stock, and German investments abroad are all named. The paper is the claim the West would argue over for years.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d471:
Twenty decisions and more are counted in this American list of what the three heads of government settled at Yalta, dated February 11, 1945. The first puts the word "dismemberment" into the German surrender terms. The second names a committee — Eden, Winant, and Gusev — to study dismemberment itself.

Next come the adoption of the American voting plan for the Security Council, and the United Nations conference set for April 25, 1945. America would consult China and France on both points, for all three powers. The list runs on to the permanent seats. As a checklist, it is the conference's balance sheet: what eight days in the Crimea had decided.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d71:
James Dunn, director of the Office of European Affairs, sent this preparation memorandum to Under Secretary Stettinius on 10 November 1944. It is titled “Preparation for Big Three Meeting” and is printed in the Malta and Yalta volume of Foreign Relations. Dunn looks ahead to the argument over the Soviet veto.

On the world organization, Dunn warns that Moscow wants a veto covering peaceful settlement as well as enforcement action. If the Russians stay adamant on the wider claim, he advises postponing any United Nations meeting for the present. A veto limited to enforcement, he argues, the United States could accept, and the American people would receive it well.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d171:
The Joint Chiefs of Staff told General Deane in Moscow what they were ready to discuss with the Russians, in a telegram dated June 27, 1945. The message is document 171 in the Foreign Relations volume on the Potsdam Conference. Military talks between the Americans and the Soviets were expected beside the main conference.

The chiefs will be ready, they say, to swap estimates of the Japanese situation and to discuss plans for the war against Japan, so the two sides can coordinate. They will gladly take up other proper subjects the Russians wish to raise. Deane is told to ask the Soviet General Staff to advise Washington soon which further subjects it wants on the table. The telegram set the terms for the first U.S.-Soviet staff talks of the Potsdam period.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d271:
Acting Secretary Grew forwarded a report on Vienna's mood in a letter dated July 9, 1945. The letter and its enclosure extracts form document 271 in the Foreign Relations volume on the Potsdam Conference. The report came from Ambassador Murphy and rested on the questioning of a member of the Vienna Philharmonic Orchestra who had crossed into the American zone.

The informant described a violent reaction among Viennese against the Soviet troops. The Russians, he reported, were agitating with every propaganda agency at their disposal. An election was expected, probably not until fall, and the Russians were working toward election day night and day. Grew thought the Secretary would want the report before him, and perhaps laid before the President, as the delegation left for Potsdam.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d371: Grew's cable to Pauley of July 8, 1945, is a holding answer, and it is printed in full. Instead of replying now to the questions raised in Pauley's message of July 5, the Secretary suggests a different course. These issues, he writes, should be discussed and decided when Pauley joins the President at Berlin. The brief note pushed the open reparations fights, France's share among them, up to the heads of government themselves.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d471:
Field Marshal Alexander's rebuke of a British treaty draft is reported in an extract of Kirk's cable from Caserta of July 15, 1945. During his recent London visit, Churchill had asked Alexander to confer with Foreign Office officials on the proposed peace treaty with Italy. With Eden ill, Alexander talked with Sargent. After studying the draft carefully, he gave his verdict.

The draft, Alexander told the Foreign Office, was far too severe, and he could not concur in it. Tripoli, he believed, should now be returned to Italy definitely and without strings. Eritrea and Italian Somaliland should also go back, with certain conditions attached. He added that Italy should be given a small fleet, excellent for her morale.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d571:
The Acting Secretary of State, Joseph Grew, wired Belgrade charge Harold Shantz on June 25, 1945. The secret message is document 571 in volume one of the Foreign Relations papers on the Potsdam Conference. It tells Shantz how to answer Tito's claim that civil rule in Venezia Giulia was still pending.

Grew calls that claim hard to grasp in light of article 3 of the Belgrade agreement. Shantz is to press this view on Yugoslav officials in his talks. He is also to keep one thought before them at all times. Good will in the United States for just Yugoslav claims, Grew warns, will rest largely on strict keeping of signed pledges.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d671:
Ambassador Armour in Madrid pushed back against inviting Moscow into the Tangier talks on July 9, 1945. His urgent confidential wire is document 671 in volume one of the Foreign Relations papers on Potsdam. It answers Washington's wire of July 5, printed as document 667.

Armour agrees Moscow should not be given the sense that the western powers act alone. But he cannot see how an active Soviet role is justified while small statute powers are kept out. Those states, he argues, have an inescapable interest in any change at Tangier. They ran the zone's administration with others before Spain seized it. Their interest grows if great powers with little direct stake settle the zone's fate in their absence. Armour also reads Washington's wire to mean Russians would join the interim occupation itself, a step he questions.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d71:
President Truman answered Churchill's plan for a royal visit to Berlin in a telegram extract dated June 16, 1945. The extract is document 71 in the Foreign Relations papers on the Potsdam Conference. Churchill had proposed that King George VI spend a day in Berlin during the conference, lunching with the Russians and dining with the other heads of state.

Truman's surviving lines are brief and warm. He says he will be very pleased to agree to any arrangements Churchill makes to carry out the King's wishes during the visit. The rest of the message is not printed. The reply left the plan in British hands and kept the King's role, a social rather than political one, on track for the conference weeks.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1071:
Ambassador Lincoln MacVeagh sent this long despatch from Athens to the Secretary of State on July 17, 1945. It transmits a survey of conditions in northern Greece by Third Secretary Leonard Cromie. A second report, on the British Army in Greece, was written by Captain William McNeill, who toured Macedonia and western Thrace with Cromie in June.

Cromie's findings do not back claims of anarchy and wholesale terror in the north. The picture matches the rest of Greece, with sharper republican feeling in the cities. Prison figures do show weak courts and royalist officials who slight the civil rights of leftists. Some Slavophones have fled across the Yugoslav border. The reports credit British officers with working to restore order and fair treatment.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1171:
President Truman wrote straight to Generalissimo Stalin on 20 July 1945. A note between the two leaders was the summit's highest channel. No staff drafted the meaning, however clerks may have typed the words; the principals spoke for themselves.

Mid-conference, such a message could praise, press, warn, or smooth a rough point between sessions. Each word in it was weighed in both camps. This exchange is leader-level dealing in a single note. It shows the personal track that ran beside the formal talks, and on which some of Potsdam's hardest points were truly settled.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1271:
The British Chiefs of Staff issued this memorandum on 22 July 1945. It is the third of their papers in this stretch of the volume. The British staff's run of notes kept London's team supplied with the soldiers' view through the summit's turn into its second week.

Staff papers of this kind weighed forces and fronts in plain terms. They told the envoys what the services could do, and what they could not. This memorandum does that work at its date. In sequence, the British notes show a staff machine matching the American one paper for paper, across the same crowded days.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1371:
Admiral William Leahy, the president's chief of staff, set down a memorandum on 24 July 1945. Leahy stood closer to Truman day by day than almost any other officer in Washington or Potsdam. Foreign Relations of the United States, the official American diplomatic record, prints it in the second volume on the Potsdam Conference.

Leahy's papers carry weight because he heard everything and said little in public. A memorandum from his hand records how a question looked from the president's own doorway. Readers tracing the summit's inner workings watch for Leahy entries the way they watch for the president's. Rarely long, often placed at turns in the story. This one belongs to the busy days just before the conference issued its call to Japan.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d710a-71:
Churchill's own note stands in for a missing United States record in volume two of the Potsdam papers. No U.S. record of this conversation has been found, the editors say. The note by Churchill is reprinted from Ehrman's official history, Grand Strategy.

Churchill's note reports what Byrnes told him that morning, apparently July 23, 1945. Byrnes had cabled to T. V. Soong, the Chinese negotiator in Moscow. He advised Soong not to give way on any point to the Russians. Soong should instead return to Moscow and keep negotiating, pending further developments. Churchill drew a blunt conclusion from the news, and the note quotes it in full. It is quite clear, he wrote, that the United States does not at present desire Russian participation in the war against Japan. The editors cite the cable itself later in the volume.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d771:
Document 771 is a Soviet proposal tabled on July 30, 1945, two days before the close. Soviet endgame texts held the lines Moscow valued most. This one entered the numbered record of the second Potsdam volume. It stands beside American and British drafts of the same final days.

A late Soviet proposal lets readers test the final bargain. What the protocol granted and refused can be read off such texts. The document shows Moscow still pressing as the clock ran down. It also shows the discipline of the Soviet team: positions stated in writing, defended to the end. The paper is a key witness to the closing trades.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d871:
Secretary of War Henry Stimson sent this memorandum to the President on July 22, 1945, during the Potsdam Conference. He titles it the rehabilitation of Europe as a whole. Stimson writes that war has destroyed moral values across the continent, not just property and wealth.

Stimson urges that Germany be given a chance to live and work. Controls, he argues, should go only as far as basic aims require. He also asks for one coordinated plan for all of Europe. American aid, surplus goods, and bank credits should flow through a single agency. He proposes an Economic Council for Europe, chaired by an American, to guide the work.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d971:
Drafting committee members weighed this reparations text at Potsdam in late July 1945. The heading calls it agreed, with reserves noted. Soviet claims would come from the Soviet zone, and Poland's claims from the Soviet share. Western claims would come from the western zones and German external assets, both points reserved by the Soviet delegate.

The USSR would further receive 15 percent of surplus western equipment in trade, and 10 percent more free of charge. The amount must be set within six months, and removals finished within two years of that ruling. A closing line has the Soviet government renounce claims to western securities, external assets, and German gold.
frus-1977-80v11p1-d271: A 1977-1980 FRUS document from the Iran hostage crisis volume. The embassy seizure. This entry preserves that record. Those who study the era will use it. The archive keeps the paper open to all. Its pages add to the record of the past.
gao-gaoreports-b-310971: This 2008 decision resolves a federal contract protest filed by Colson Services Corporation. Losing bidders can ask GAO to review whether an agency ran the competition fairly. Agencies almost always follow these rulings, which build the case law for federal contracts.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-271: The Joint Strike Fighter needed a safer buying plan in 2005, and GAO's report says a different acquisition strategy could reduce risks. The review rewrites the playbook. The trillion-dollar jet deserved the caution. The strategy had to change. The trillion-dollar jet deserved the caution.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-371: Agent Orange's civilian victims stayed uncounted in 2005, and GAO's report says the toll on non-soldiers was unknown. The review admits the data gap plainly. The hurt deserved the true count badly. The hurt deserved the true count badly. The count was missing.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-471: Federal IPv6 transition needed planning in 2005, and GAO's report says agencies had to plan and manage security risks. The findings demand the roadmap. The report warns that the internet's next chapter deserved doing right. The planning had to be done.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-671: The IRS's output gauges needed sharpening in 2005, and GAO's report says fresh methods could tune the math. The findings demand the upgrade. The report warns that the tax agency's output deserved honest measuring. The tax agency's output deserved honest measuring.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-971: A Colombian oil line saw fewer bombings in 2005, and GAO's report says the guard effort cut the strikes, though woes stayed. The findings balance credit and need. The report warns that the pipeline deserved guarding. The pipeline deserved guarding. The guard effort had to hold.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-171: The Pentagon's asset deployment system had marginal value in 2006, and GAO's report says uncertain joint use and weak expected value warranted review. The findings question the investment. The report warns that the logistics software needed justifying. The value had to be proven.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-271: High-deductible federal health plans got a first-year review in 2006, and GAO's report examines the experience with the new options. The findings take the measure. The report warns that the workers' health gambles needed watching. The experience had to be studied.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-471: Undeclared hazardous shipments got new DOT attention in 2006, and GAO's report says the new efforts might reveal more about the hidden cargo. The findings track the start. The report warns that the secret dangerous goods needed daylight. The efforts had to continue.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-571: Jumbo-jet airport upgrades cost a fortune in 2006, and GAO's report examines the costs and factors for accommodating the superjumbo. The findings do the math. The report warns that the giant planes needed giant gates. The costs had to be faced.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-771: Immigration courts' caseload reporting needed work in 2006, and GAO's report says the performance reporting wanted improvement. The findings target the numbers. The report warns that the backlogged courts needed honest scorecards. The reporting had to improve. The courts' numbers had to be honest.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-1071: A 2007 Government Accountability Office report finding the Export-Import Bank needed to improve how it assessed the economic impact of its financing. The bank subsidizes American exports, but GAO questioned whether its impact analyses were rigorous. The report presses for better measurement of whether the bank's deals truly benefit the U.S. economy or mainly benefit the companies receiving them.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-371: The bank insurance funds got an audit in 2007, and GAO's report grades the FDIC funds' financial statements for 2006 and 2005. The findings deliver the formal opinion. The report shows the deposit guardian's own books get checked. The insurer's vault got its own inspection.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-671: Moving military families was a logistical tangle in 2007 — GAO's report says the Pentagon needed one coherent plan for its new household-goods system. The findings target the moving-day mess. The report's demand: plan the move like the mission depends on it, because morale does.
gao-gaoreports-gao-08-71: GAO's 2007 report revisits the poisoned town of Libby, Montana — and the far-flung sites that took its tainted ore. GAO says the EPA may need to re-grade those sites and must do better at warning the neighbors. The report keeps the heat on one of America's grimmest toxics sagas, where the cleanup's loose ends still threatened lives.
gao-gaoreports-gao-08-871: In 2008, the Government Accountability Office published this report on pension Benefit Guaranty Corporation: Some Steps Have Been Taken to Improve Contracting, but a More Strategic Approach is Needed. GAO is Congress's watchdog, and its work lays out what the team found and what should change. Its conclusions can shape how agencies run their programs.
german-empire-constitution-1871:
The Constitution of the German Empire took effect in 1871, weeks after the empire was proclaimed at Versailles. Otto von Bismarck, Prussia's chancellor, drafted the charter to bind Germany's princes into one Reich without breaking their thrones. German unity had been won by war; the constitution gave that victory lasting legal form.

The text makes the king of Prussia German emperor by right, and gives the empire power over war, trade, railways, and law. A federal council of state governments faces a Reichstag elected by all adult men, though the chancellor answers to the emperor, not to parliament. Prussia's weight runs through the whole design. The empire's founding statute ruled Germany until the crash of 1918. Its mix of democracy below and authority above defined the Reich that Bismarck built.
goethe-faust-part-2-taylor-1871:
Bayard Taylor completed his metrical Faust with Part Two in 1871. The Osgood first edition gave English readers the first great rendering of the sequel. Goethe had finished the vast second part near the end of his life.

Faust moves through courts, classical myths, and grand schemes of land and sea. Helen of Troy appears, and strange spirits crowd the crowded stage action. The scope is huge, part pageant, part deep thought on man's striving. Faust dies old and blind, still reaching for one good shared work. Taylor's feat let English readers grasp the whole design at last.
govdocs-archive_org-SonsOfLibertyRobertJ:
In September 2005 the Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco, Firearms and Explosives answered a Freedom of Information request from researcher Ernie Lazar. The release gathers disclosable portions of FBI-originated documents on Robert Jay Mathews and the Sons of Liberty.

Mathews founded The Order, a white-supremacist group whose crime spree ended with his death in 1984, and the files track official interest in him and his circle. Names and passages are withheld where the law allows, as FOIA releases usually are. The library presents the file as a public record, without endorsement, for researchers of the American far right.
govdocs-archive_org-lainedByTheLivSchoup:
Rev. F. X. Schouppe, a French Jesuit, wrote Purgatory Explained by the Lives and Legends of the Saints to teach Catholic doctrine on the afterlife through stories. This copy is the TAN Books pocketbook reprint of 1986, taken from the 1893 Benziger edition.

Schouppe builds his teaching from reported apparitions, visions, and legends of the saints, in which souls in purgatory ask the living for prayers. Each story is followed by the doctrine it illustrates: suffering, prayer, and the bond between the living and the dead. The book was a devotional classic, and the cheap reprint kept it in Catholic homes.
hartmann-erec-haupt-1871:
Hartmann von Aue wrote Erec, the first Arthurian romance in German, in the years around 1200. Moriz Haupt's 1871 edition prints the medieval German text in full, all 10,135 verses of it. The knight Erec stands at the center of the tale.

Erec wins a bride and high honor, then sinks into sloth and lets his name fall. Shamed by his wife's grief, he rides out with her to win his honor back through hard trials. The poem set the pattern for German courtly romance for two full centuries. Haupt's text is the classic school edition of the work.
hunter-natural-history-teeth-1771:
Teeth got their first scientific account in John Hunter's Natural History of the Human Teeth, from 1771. Hunter dissected jaws and teeth at every age of life. He describes how teeth form, grow, and sit in their sockets. Structure comes first, then the diseases that attack it.

Decay, gum trouble, and the ills of teething all receive ordered treatment. His plates show the parts with a clarity earlier books lacked. The work founded scientific dentistry as a field of study. Practitioners gained a base in anatomy rather than craft lore alone. The first edition keeps his terms and figures intact. Modern dentists can still read him with profit.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-lublinsky-solom:
Solomon Lublinsky, a German journalist and writer, was born at Johannisberg, Prussia, on February 18, 1868. He is profiled in a Jewish Encyclopedia entry from 1906 by Herman Rosenthal and A. S. Waldstein. He worked for a time as a clerk in a second-hand bookstore at Venice. He then took up journalism at Berlin.

By 1904, the article says, Lublinsky stood among the foremost Jewish writers. Beyond his newspaper work, it lists his Berlin books: a study of Jewish characters in Grillparzer, Hebbel, and Ludwig, and a work on literature and society in the nineteenth century. It also lists the dramas “Multatuli,” “Der Imperator,” and “Hannibal.” A novel, “Gescheitert,” appeared in 1901. The entry is brief, but it fixes the shape of a young career split between journalism, criticism, and the stage.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-magnus-eduard-1:
Eduard Magnus, a German painter, receives a biographical entry in the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. Born at Berlin on January 7, 1799, he tried medicine, architecture, and philosophy first. He settled at last on painting, training at the Berlin Academy of Fine Arts. He died at Berlin on August 8, 1872.

The article follows his travels and his fame. He spent years in France and Italy, and later toured Spain as well. In 1837 he joined the Berlin Academy, and in 1841 he was named professor. His broad culture gave him real influence in art circles. He is best known for portraits, including Jenny Lind, Mendelssohn-Bartholdy, and Count Wrangel. His genre scenes range from a fisher boy of Nice to Italian landscapes. Orders and gold medals marked his success. The entry preserves a portraitist at the center of Berlin's art world.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-mannheimer-hers:
Louise Mannheimer, born Herschman, a writer and poet, is profiled in the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. Born at Prague on September 3, 1845, she crossed to New York with her parents in 1866. There she married Professor Sigmund Mannheimer. She wrote poems in both German and English.

The article lists her work for two audiences at once. German and English periodicals carried her poems, articles, and reviews. Her English renderings include a translation of one of Judah ha-Levi's poems, titled The Storm. The Harvest, her own prize poem, appeared in an American Jews' annual in 1897. In 1895 she published The Jewish Woman, her translation of Nahida Remy's book on Jewish womanhood. She also founded the Cincinnati Jewish Industrial School for Boys. A patent ventilator of her invention rounds out the entry's portrait of a versatile writer.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-master-and-serv:
Master and servant means the duties of employers toward hired workers. Isidore Singer and Lewis N. Dembitz treat it in a Jewish Encyclopedia article from 1906. Its foundation is the wage rule of the Pentateuch. The hire of a workman must not stay with the employer overnight. Deuteronomy adds that he be paid on the very day he earns it, before the sun goes down.

From there the article builds the rabbinic law of labor out of the Mishnah. Field hands might eat grapes or corn where they worked, but they could not carry any away. Hours and meals followed local custom, so no employer could demand dawn or evening work where that was not the practice. A famous story of R. Johanan ben Mattai warns employers on this point. Even a feast like Solomon's would not free one who had promised more than bread and beans.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-meir-moses-meir:
Meir ben Ephraim of Padua, called Moses Meir, was a scribe and printer at Mantua. Joseph Jacobs and Ismar Elbogen profile him in the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. After trying various trades he settled as a scribe, and a superlative one. Forty-three of his Torah scrolls stood in Italian communities. The first was finished in 1541 and the last begun in 1582, the year before his death.

His model scroll, with its long colophon of commissions, was still kept by the Mantua community. In 1556 he founded a printing house at Mantua. It did brave service while the Inquisition hunted Hebrew books. From his press came handy editions of the Mishnah, the Shulhan Aruk, and the code of Maimonides. It printed the treatises of the Talmud, and, most famous of all, the first edition of the Zohar, in 1558 to 1560.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-mendes-maurits-:
Maurits Benjamin da Costa Mendes was a Dutch classical philologist. Isidore Singer and E. Slijper profile him in the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He was born at Amsterdam in 1851. He entered the Athenaeum to study classics. But a gymnasium accident worsened the deafness he had had since boyhood. It broke off his regular studies. He made his way as a private teacher of languages and gained a name for teaching. From 1891 he kept the manuscripts of the university library.

His fame is Homeric. With Van Leeuwen he produced the "Editio Batavorum" of the Iliad and Odyssey. The edition restores the lost letter digamma wherever comparative grammar proved it had once sounded. School grammars of Attic and of the Homeric idiom followed, translated into German and French. Amsterdam made him an honorary doctor in 1898. The entry closes with his second love, the stage. For the stage he wrote and translated plays.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-mezei-ernest-10:
Ernest Mezei, born at Satoralja-Ujhely in Hungary in May 1851, was a journalist and member of parliament profiled in a Jewish Encyclopedia entry by Isidore Singer and Gabriel Weiss. He studied law and philosophy at Budapest and wrote for the Ellenör while still a student. In 1874 he helped found the opposition daily Egyetértés and stayed on its staff.

Backed by Louis Kossuth, Mezei lost a first run for parliament in 1878 but won the Miskolcz seat in 1881. When the Tisza-Eszlár blood accusation inflamed Hungary, he challenged the minister of justice in the House and spoke hard against the anti-Semites. He also wrote poems, an 1877 book of Italian travels, and a lecture opposing Zionism as a national program.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-mirels-meshulla:
Meshullam Zalman ben David Neumark Mirels, born at Vienna about 1620, was a German rabbi whose life followed the expulsions of his age. Gotthard Deutsch and S. Mannheimer wrote his Jewish Encyclopedia entry in 1906. When Vienna expelled its Jews in 1670, he emigrated to Berlin with his son Zeeb Wolf and the wider Mirels family.

In 1678 Mirels became chief rabbi of the triple community of Altona, Hamburg, and Wandsbeck, and held the post until his death in 1706. He lived to see a fifth generation of descendants spread through Poland and Lithuania. His daughter Sarah married Ẓebi Ashkenazi, the Ḥakam Ẓebi, and was mother of Jacob Emden; of his writing, one responsum survives in print.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-monuments-in-th:
Monuments in their bearing on biblical exegesis argues a revolution in evidence, in a Jewish Encyclopedia article from the Executive Committee of the Editorial Board published in 1906. For centuries the Old Testament's authenticity had to be argued from inside its own pages. Now the nations around Israel have risen from the dead with archives of their own.

Egypt and Babylonia, the article shows, had schools, libraries, and literature long before Abraham; under Hammurabi, Babylon was reediting its classics while Egypt read the Proverbs of Ptah-hotep. The monuments give the biblical books a contemporary literature to be tested against — as much external witness for Moses' age, the writers claim, as for Pericles' Athens. Archaeology here becomes a tool of exegesis.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-moses-of-crete-:
Moses of Crete was a false Messiah of the middle fifth century. The Jewish Encyclopedia entry, by its editorial committee and M. Seligsohn, tells a grim story. In those years many Jews expected the Messiah in the eighty-fifth jubilee. An enthusiast whose real name is unknown took the name Moses and toured the island for a year.

He convinced the congregations of Crete that he was the expected one. Awaiting the day, the Jews neglected their affairs and abandoned their property. On the appointed day he led them to a promontory and ordered them to throw themselves down, promising the waters would divide. Many drowned; sailors rescued others, and Moses was never seen again.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-moss-lucien-111:
Lucien Moss was an American philanthropist of Philadelphia, born there on May 25, 1831. Cyrus Adler and Frederick T. Haneman wrote his Jewish Encyclopedia entry. Trained as a machinist, he set up sugar mills in Porto Rico for a Philadelphia firm. Later he founded Wiler and Moss, brass workers, and retired in 1878.

His later years went to charity. Moss served on the boards of the Hebrew charitable societies of Philadelphia and of the societies against cruelty to animals and to children. He left the bulk of his moderate fortune to the Jewish Hospital Association. The gift founded the Lucien Moss Home for Incurables of the Jewish Faith, and he died in 1895.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-nagdela-nagrela:
Joseph ibn Nagdela was a Spanish statesman who succeeded his father Samuel as vizier of Granada. Richard Gottheil and Meyer Kayserling wrote his Jewish Encyclopedia entry. Born about 1031, he was highly educated and directed an important school. He aided many students, among them the Talmudist Isaac ibn Albalia and the poet Isaac ibn Ghayyat.

Unlike his father, Joseph was proud and ruled the drunken King Badis completely, filling offices with his coreligionists. Berber hatred built around him, fanned by a hostile poem and a rumor of treason. In 1066 a mob stormed the palace; Joseph, hidden in a coal pit with a blackened face, was found and killed. Most of Granada's Jews perished with him.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-nathan-ben-samu:
Nathan ben Samuel was a Spanish doctor who also wrote on the Bible. His entry was written by the Editorial Board's Executive Committee and S. Kahn for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He flourished early in the fourteenth century, as far as is known. Manuscripts give his name in a short form read two ways. One reading makes him a Tibbon by family name.

About 1307 he wrote a Pentateuch study called Zikkaron Tob. A shortened form survives as Mibhar ha-Ma'amarim, printed at Leghorn in 1840. The entry warns against mixing him up with another Nathan. That man was a Montpellier doctor of the century before. Scholars link that doctor to Nathan ben Joel Falaquera instead. The care with names is the heart of the entry.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-neumann-isidor-:
Isidor Neumann was an Austrian doctor of skin diseases. Isidore Singer and Frederick T. Haneman wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He was born at Misslitz, Moravia, on March 2, 1832. He was educated at the University of Vienna. He took his medical degree in 1858.

Vienna made him privat-docent three years later. In 1873 he rose to assistant professor there. In 1881 he became professor of dermatology outright. He also directed the clinic for syphilis at Vienna. His textbook of skin diseases appeared in 1868. A fifth edition had come by 1880. He wrote on the skin's lymph vessels in 1873. An atlas of skin diseases followed in 1881. His textbook of syphilis appeared six years later.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-noah-11571:
Noah stands ninth in descent from Adam. Six hands wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. They include McCurdy, Bacher, Hirsch, and Montgomery. Amid wide corruption he alone walked with God. Scripture calls him righteous and blameless in his generations.

God warned him of a flood to destroy all flesh. He built an ark three hundred cubits long. Eight souls entered it, with pairs of every creature. Rain fell forty days and the waters prevailed. The ark rested at last on Ararat's mountains. Noah sent out a raven, then a dove. The dove returned bearing an olive leaf. His altar won a covenant sealed by the rainbow. Blood was banned, and man's blood demanded man's life. He died at nine hundred and fifty years.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-ornament-11771:
Ornament treats the jewels and dress trim of Bible times. Emil G. Hirsch and Wilhelm Nowack wrote the entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. Both men and women wore such trim in old lands. It held the same high place then as now. In the East, that love of trim lives on.

Rich men wore trim, the piece says, as a rule. The poorest woman still found some trim to wear. A rich woman was known by the count of her jewels. The Bible names a host of such goods by name. Ear rings and nose rings are both named there. Drop shaped ear jewels are named as netifot. The necklace was worn by women and by men. It was made of more than one chain of gold.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-palgrave-cohen-:
Sir Francis Palgrave was an English writer on the past. Joseph Jacobs wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He was born in London in July of 1788. He died there on July 6, in 1861. His father was Meyer Cohen, of the London stock mart.

Francis was a child of rare gifts from the start. At eight he put a Homer tale into French verse. That work was put out in print by his father. In 1823 he changed his name by royal leave. He took the name Palgrave in place of Cohen then. He trained as a lawyer and joined the bar in 1827. His heart lay with the old records of his land. For ten years he brought out books of those records. In 1838 he became the keeper of the queen's records.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-pearl-11971:
The pearl was a prized gem long before the Bible was closed. Four writers shared this article in the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. They were Emil G. Hirsch, Wilhelm Nowack, the Executive Committee, and M. Seligsohn. Ancient trade drew pearls from three warm seas.

Those seas were the Indian Ocean, the Persian Gulf, and the Red Sea. Whether the Bible names the pearl is left in doubt. Two rare Hebrew words may mean pearls or red coral. The rabbis told of a pearl found inside a fish. They ranked the Persians as the best pearl fishers.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-pinner-adolf-12:
Adolf Pinner was a German chemist of wide research range. Isidore Singer and Frederick T. Haneman wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He was born at Wronke on August 31, 1842. He took his chemistry doctorate at Berlin in 1867. The state gave him a privy councillor's title.

Pinner taught chemistry at Berlin's university and veterinary college. In 1884 he joined the German patent office. His papers treat nicotine, pilocarpine, and acetone compounds. His book on imido-ethers gathered years of journal work. His chemistry handbook ran to eleven editions. It was translated into English, Russian, and Japanese.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-raphael-frederi:
Frederick Melchior Raphael was an English soldier born in London in 1870. Joseph Jacobs and Goodman Lipkind wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906. He was educated at Wellington College. He died at Spion Kop on January 24, 1900.

The article traces his rise through the Rifle Brigade. He entered the regular army in 1891. He became a lieutenant in 1893 and a captain in 1898. He trained in signaling, map work, and musketry teaching. In November 1899 his regiment sailed for South Africa. He led 130 men and a machine gun there. He was killed in Warren's fight with the Boers. The entry is a brief record of a short army life.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-remainders-and-:
Remainders and reversions are terms from Anglo-American property law. Wilhelm Bacher and Lewis N. Dembitz wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906. A remainder is a future share granted to another person. A reversion is the share a grantor keeps back.

The article says these words are unknown to Jewish law. Yet similar interests could arise under it in limited ways. A landowner could sell land for a term of years. He could also sell only its produce for years. A gift for life raised fewer doubts than a sale. Maimonides shows such grants in trees, dovecotes, and hives. Even unborn young and unmade honey could be included. The entry tests English terms against Talmudic practice.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-rishonim-lit-th:
Rishonim means the first ones, or the elders. Isidore Singer and Jacob Zallel Lauterbach wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906. The name applies to authorities who lived before the writer quoting them. In the Talmud it simply means predecessor or ancestor.

The article explains the narrower later use of the term. Later rabbinical writing reserves it for authorities before the Shulhan Aruk. All authorities from that code onward are called aharonim. That word means the later ones, in contrast. Three Talmud passages show the older, looser sense. Shabbat, Berakot, and Tamid are cited for it. A cross reference sends readers to the Aharonim entry. The short piece fixes a term students meet everywhere. Knowing the split helps date any quoted authority.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-rosenthal-juliu:
Julius Rosenthal was an American lawyer born in Baden, Germany, on September 17, 1828. Cyrus Adler and Joseph Stolz wrote his entry for the 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia. Educated at Heidelberg and Freiburg, he emigrated to Chicago in 1854.

Rosenthal worked in a bank, studied law, and joined the bar in 1860. He served as public administrator of Cook County for twenty-five years. He helped direct Chicago's first public library board in 1872. For decades he ran the Chicago Law Institute's library and once presided over it. He was also a founder of Sinai Congregation and backed many relief societies.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-sabinus-12971:
Sabinus was a Roman procurator and treasurer sent by Augustus to Judea. Joseph Jacobs and Schulim Ochser wrote his entry for the 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia. In 4 B.C. he came to inventory the estate left by Herod.

Sabinus broke his promise to Varus and hurried on to Jerusalem. His harsh oppression sparked a revolt during the week of Pentecost. The Jews besieged him in the tower Phasaelus, above the city. Roman troops fired the Temple colonnade, killing many Jews trapped there. Sabinus himself, Josephus says, took 400 talents of gold from the treasury.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-samson-13071:
Samson is one of the judges of Israel, whose acts fill Judges chapters thirteen to sixteen. Joseph Jacobs, Ira Maurice Price, Wilhelm Bacher, and Jacob Zallel Lauterbach wrote the entry for the 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia. His story unfolds under Philistine oppression of Israel.

An angel promised Samson to Manoah and his barren wife at Zorah. The child must be a Nazarite: no wine, and no razor on his head. Grown, he fell for a Philistine woman of Timnah and married her. At the wedding feast he posed a riddle to thirty companions. His bride drew out its answer and betrayed it to them.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-sanctuary-13171:
Judah David Eisenstein wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, issued with the Executive Committee of the Editorial Board in 1906. It explains the sanctuary, a sacred place for divine service. Jewish tradition counts six sanctuaries in all. The first was the Tabernacle Moses built in the wilderness. Others stood at Shiloh, at Nob, and at Gibeon. Then came the First Temple and the Second Temple at Jerusalem.

The Tabernacle, like the Temple, held the holy Ark with the tablets of the covenant. Only purified priests could enter its inner rooms. Sacrifices could be offered there and nowhere else. Yet even the sanctuary gave no shelter to a murderer. The article quotes God's words in Exodus. The sanctuary was made so that God might dwell among the people. One central shrine also bound the twelve tribes into one nation.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-schill-solomon-:
Isidore Singer and Ludwig Venetianer wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia entry, published in 1906, on Solomon Schill. He was a Hungarian philologist, a scholar of languages. Schill was born on October 14, 1849, in Budapest. He studied at Raab, Budapest, and Vienna. He won his diploma as a teacher. In 1874 he became a professor at the gymnasium at Arad.

In 1878 Schill moved to the rabbinical seminary at Budapest. He teaches Latin and Greek there still in 1905. All of his books are written in Hungarian. They include a Greek grammar and Greek exercises. He also wrote on Greek antiquities and Greek art. His history of Greek literature went through three editions. He turned Philo's account of the embassy to Caligula into Hungarian. He also translated Genesis, Exodus, and Deuteronomy, plus the prayer book.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-shabbethai-be-e: Shabbethai Be'er, also called Fonte, was an Italian rabbi of the seventeenth century. Gotthard Deutsch and S. Mannheimer wrote the 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia entry on him. He is known for one book, Be'er Esek, printed at Venice in 1674. That book gathers 112 of his responsa, his formal answers to questions on Jewish law sent to him. Two standard reference works, Conforte and Steinschneider, preserve the record of his work.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-shetar-deed-plu:
Shetar is the Hebrew word for a deed, with the plural shetarot. Joseph Jacobs wrote the 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia entry on these documents. Ancient rules for drawing deeds carried into medieval practice. Most Jewish deeds then recorded debts owed by Christian borrowers.

Such deeds usually came with a Latin translation attached. They followed the forms of local royal chancelleries. In England and Germany many bilingual deeds survive. The Latin name for the form was starrum, from the Hebrew. Some think Westminster's Star Chamber took its name from stored starra. English deeds were often parchment tallies called chirographs. Standard contract forms were gathered by Judah ben Barzillai and others. The entry links paper, debt, and Jewish life under Christian rule.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-singer-edmund-1:
Edmund Singer was a Hungarian violinist born at Totis on October 14, 1831. Isidore Singer and Joseph Sohn wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906. He studied under Ellinger, Ridley Kohne, and Joseph Böhm. He also learned composition from Preyer. From 1844 to 1846 he studied at the Paris Conservatoire.

In 1846 Singer became concert-master at the Stadttheater in Budapest. He then toured Europe with great success for three years. On Liszt's advice he took the same post at Weimar in 1854. He stayed there until 1861. Since then he has led the orchestra at Stuttgart. He also teaches at the Conservatorium in that city.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-solomon-b-judah:
Solomon ben Judah Löb of Dessau was a German Hebraist and teacher. The Executive Committee of the Editorial Board and Peter Wiernik wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906. He was born about 1662 and died after 1734. He taught at Dessau for many years. A small Hebrew vocabulary was long ascribed to him.

That work now seems to belong to another author instead. Editions of it appeared as early as 1640. His own Iggerot Shelomoh held Hebrew and Judæo-German letters. It appeared at Wandsbeck in 1732. He also described an anti-Jewish riot in Hamburg in 1730. He had witnessed that riot with his own eyes that year.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-spitz-meir-b-jo: Meir ben Johanan Spitz was rabbi of Oronie, in Hungary. The Executive Committee of the Editorial Board and Schulim Ochser wrote this brief Jewish Encyclopedia entry, published in 1906. He served there in the eighteenth century. He wrote Katit la-Ma'or, halakic novellae on Talmudic treatises. He also wrote Shemen ha-Ma'or, novellae on ritual matters. Both of his works appeared at Vienna in the year 1792.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-strashun-samuel:
Samuel Strashun was a Russian Talmudist born in the Wilna region in 1794. The Executive Committee of the Editorial Board and Peter Wiernik wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article in 1906. His father educated him at home. He took his name from Strashun, his wife's village. He died in Wilna on March 21, 1872.

Strashun's family lost its distillery to the French invasion of 1812. In Wilna he built another while his wife ran business. He gave most of his time to Talmud study and teaching. For years he lectured daily at a Wilna synagogue. Notes from those talks entered every later Babylonian Talmud edition. He refused the rabbinate of Suwalki to stay independent. The entry honors a teacher whose glosses outlived him.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-szabolcsi-max-1:
Max Szabolcsi was a Hungarian author born at Tura in 1857. Isidore Singer and Ludwig Venetianer wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article about him in 1906. He was born on August 27 of that year. In youth he studied Talmud at Budapest's seminary briefly. He wrote for Hebrew periodicals under a pen name.

Szabolcsi translated the story parts of Sanhedrin into Hungarian. His fame grew during the Tisza-Eszlár blood case. He wrote defense articles in a Debrecen newspaper then. In 1884 he took over a Jewish paper in Pest. Two years later he gained control of Egyenlöség. That weekly became his main platform at Budapest. The entry honors an editor who fought a blood libel in print. His career shows the press as a shield for Jews.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-tawus-jacob-b-j:
Jacob ben Joseph Tawus was a Persian translator of the Bible. Wilhelm Bacher wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article about him in 1906. He flourished in the sixteenth century. His surname means peacock in his tongue. Almost nothing else is known of his life.

A polyglot Pentateuch appeared at Constantinople in 1546. It printed a Persian Bible version in Hebrew letters. Its editor praised the wise and learned Tawus by name. The volume also held Onkelos and Saadia's Arabic. Moses Hamon, physician to Sultan Sulaiman, figures in its story. He likely brought Tawus himself to Constantinople. The version seems made there for that very edition. Around 1570 another Tawus appears in a responsum. The entry rescues a translator from near total obscurity.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-temple-administ:
How the Second Temple in Jerusalem was run is the subject here. Joseph Jacobs and Judah David Eisenstein wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906. It draws on the Mishnah and on Maimonides. Fifteen appointed officers managed the Temple's daily affairs.

The article names each officer and his task. One kept the seals for buying sacrifices. Others handled libations, lots, fowls, wells, gates, and music. Seven trustees and three cashiers guarded the treasury. Thirteen shofar-shaped boxes took in gifts and the half-shekel tax. A secret chamber held gifts for the worthy poor. Priests and Levites also kept a strict night watch.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-trade-unionism-:
Trade-unionism among Jewish workers grew out of mass migration from eastern Europe. Joseph Jacobs, J. de Haas, Cyrus Adler, and Isaac A. Hourwich wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906. A Jewish laboring class formed as crowds packed eastern cities. The first mainly Jewish union, for tailors, dates to 1872.

Dutch Jews had long worked the diamond and cigar trades. Both trades moved early toward factory methods. Cigar workers adopted the union idea early and in strength. In East London after 1881, clothing trades took off. Immigrants built cheap clothing, mantle, and ladies' tailoring shops. Fur and rubber trades fell largely into Jewish hands. Founders of those trades testified before a royal commission in 1902.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-ullmann-shalom-: Shalom Ullmann was a Hungarian Talmudist of the early nineteenth century. Isidore Singer and A. Kecskemeti wrote this brief Jewish Encyclopedia entry, published in 1906. He officiated as rabbi in Fürth. Later he served at Boldogasszony, a small town in Wieselburg county. That place was also called Frankirchen. His one named work is Dibre Rash, from 1826. It contains notes on various Talmudic treatises.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-vera-y-alarcon-:
Lope de Vera y Alarcon was a Spanish nobleman who died for Judaism. Joseph Jacobs and Meyer Kayserling wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia entry, published in 1906. He was born about 1619 at San Clemente. Study of Hebrew at Salamanca drew him toward the Jewish faith. He read the Psalms daily in the original.

At age twenty, Vera said the Messiah had not yet come. His own brother reported him to the Inquisition. He spent six years in prison at Valladolid. There he circumcised himself and took the name Judah the Believer. No pleading could move him to return. He was burned at the stake in 1644, reciting a psalm.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-we-shameru-and-:
We Shameru quotes Exodus on keeping the Sabbath. Cyrus Adler and Francis L. Cohen wrote this short entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. The verses are Exodus chapter thirty one, verses sixteen and seventeen. The passage is recited before the Amidah on Sabbath eve. It is repeated in the home Kiddush on Sabbath morning.

Today choirs often sing it, or voices answer each other. Older cantors declaimed it in free improvisation. They built its tune from other service melodies. The Kaddish air after the Torah reading was a favorite base. The entry prints a version by Naumbourg of Paris. It preserves a fading cantorial art.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-year-book-germa:
Year-book, or Jahrbuch in German, names a book that comes out each year. Joseph Jacobs wrote its entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. Such a book holds a year count and a review. It holds tales and news of the towns as well. That mix splits it from the plain almanac form.

The first such book seems to date to 1818. It was made for Jewish youth at Berlin then. It lived for just two years in that form. A Vienna set ran for six years after that. Top Jewish minds wrote for that Vienna book. Names like Zunz and Rapoport grace its list of hands. More sets came from Vienna, Breslau, Paris, and London. One set was made by Jacobs in the English tongue.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-zipporah-15271:
Zipporah was the daughter of Jethro and the wife of Moses. Joseph Jacobs and Schulim Ochser wrote her entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. Moses met Jethro's daughters at a well, where shepherds were driving them away. He helped them, was welcomed into the house, and received Zipporah as his wife.

On the road back to Egypt, Zipporah saved Moses from great danger, the Bible reports. Later, Jethro brought her and her children out to Moses in the wilderness. She is named once more when Miriam and Aaron fault Moses over his Ethiopian wife. The entry adds rabbinic views, which praise her beauty and conduct yet also report strain in the marriage.
joseph-of-arimathie-skeat-1871:
Joseph of Arimathie is an alliterative Middle English poem about Joseph of Arimathea and the Holy Grail. W. W. Skeat, a leading scholar of old English texts, edited it in 1871. The poem gives the Grail an English origin story.

In the Bible, Joseph buries Christ and then fades from the tale. Here he carries the holy blood across the sea to Britain. There he founds a new church in the west and becomes a missionary hero. The poem mixes prayer, travel, and marvel in driving verse. It shows how eager medieval England was to claim a sacred past of its own.
kenrick-lecture-perpetual-motion-1771: William Kenrick, an English writer and critic, gave this public talk on perpetual motion in 1771. Such talks drew crowds in the coffee house age of London. Kenrick spoke at the height of the craze for wheels that turn for ever. He took the famed claims of his day one by one and showed why each must fail. His case rests on the plain laws of weight, force, and loss in all machines. Short and sharp, the talk is a neat case of a debunk from the craze's own time.
legge-chinese-classics-vol-4-part-2-1871:
James Legge published Volume 4, Part 2 of The Chinese Classics in 1871, completing his She King, the Book of Poetry. Legge was a Scottish missionary and scholar in Hong Kong. The She King, or Classic of Poetry, is one of the five classics of China, a set of songs many ascribed to Confucius's editing.

Part 2 carries the odes onward, with Chinese text, translation, and long notes on words, customs, and history. The songs cover love, war, farming, and court life in early China. Legge's version was the first full English translation of the Classic of Poetry. His notes made the poems usable by readers with no Chinese, and they stayed standard for generations.
maine-village-communities-1871:
Henry Maine, the legal historian who wrote Ancient Law, gave six lectures on village communities that appeared in 1871. He compares villages in India, Russia, and England as the oldest unit of law and property. The book extends his comparative method to land itself.

Maine argues that land was first held by groups, not by single owners, and that private property grew slowly from the kin group. Indian villages under British rule give him living evidence for Europe's past. His famous line, that law moves from status to contract, guides the lectures. Few books have shaped legal history and anthropology together as this one did.
marx-civil-war-france-1871:
Marx wrote The Civil War in France in English in 1871, as Paris burned. The address went to the General Council of the International, the workers' body he helped lead. Its subject is the Paris Commune, the brief workers' government of that spring. Marx hails the Commune as a new form of rule.

He describes how the Communards governed, fought, and fell to the Versailles army. The Commune, he argues, was the first dictatorship of the proletariat in history. That reading founded the Marxist account of the event. The prose burns with the nearness of the fighting. It remains his most famous piece of current history.
memoirs-of-louis-xiv-and-his-court-and-o:
Volume twelve of Saint-Simon's memoirs opens at chapter eighty eight. The Abbe Alberoni now governs Spain like a master, Saint-Simon says. He rose by the path of the Princesse des Ursins before him.

Alberoni plans to drive all strangers from the West Indies trade. At home he cuts the costs of the royal household. A strong navy, he holds, must ground the power of Spain. He keeps the King and Queen shut in, with the key in his pocket. He lived on fifty pistoles a month from Parma, he boasted. That show of plain life hid a grasp for a cardinal's hat.
metallographia-or-an-history-of-metals-w:
John Webster, a practitioner in physic and surgery, published this history of metals in London in 1671. The book explains the signs of ores and minerals before and after digging. It also covers how metals form, their kinds, and their differences. Webster gathered his material from Greek, Latin, and German authors.

Webster adds observations and discoveries of his own to the survey. He also takes up the hardest questions of mystical chemistry. These include the philosophers' gold, their mercury, and the universal solvent called Alkahest. The result mixes early geology, mining lore, and alchemy in one ambitious volume.
milton-paradise-regained-1671:
John Milton published Paradise Regained in 1671, a brief epic in four books. It answers Paradise Lost with a tale of trial, not fall. The subject is Christ in the wilderness, tempted by Satan after his baptism.

Satan offers bread, wealth, glory, and kingdoms to the fasting Christ. Each offer is calm, firm proof of a mind that cannot be moved. Milton keeps the tone spare, grave, and stripped of ornament. The end sends Satan fallen and Christ fed by angels in peace. Readers prize its restraint, the still and thoughtful twin of the far grander epic.
milton-samson-agonistes-1671:
John Milton published Samson Agonistes in 1671, in the same book as Paradise Regained. The text here comes from H. C. Beeching's Oxford edition of 1900. Milton shaped it as a Greek-style tragedy meant for reading, not the stage.

Samson, blind and jailed in Gaza, is mocked by Philistine lords. His wife Dalila and his father Manoa visit him in his shame. A feast summons him to perform, and he pulls the temple down. Foe and hero die in one vast ruin of stone and dust. Milton, blind himself, gave Samson's grief a stark personal force.
mivart-on-the-genesis-of-species-1871:
St. George Jackson Mivart, a Catholic biologist and skilled anatomist, published On the Genesis of Species in 1871. Once close to Darwin's circle, he turned critic of natural selection. His attack came from inside biology, not from theology alone.

Mivart argues that selection cannot explain the first stages of new structures. He points to convergence and to sudden changes in the record. Darwin answered him in the sixth edition of the Origin. Their friendship never recovered. The book remains the sharpest scientific challenge Darwin faced from a former ally. The argument forced evolution's defenders to sharpen their own case in reply.
morte-arthure-alliterative-brock-1871:
The alliterative Morte Arthure is a Middle English poem by an unknown author, retold in the pounding verse style of the north. E. Brock edited it in 1871. Its Arthur is a war leader first and a courtly king second.

Arthur marches to war against Rome itself, after the emperor demands tribute from Britain. He wins battle after battle and is close to taking an empire. Then word comes that Mordred, left in charge at home, has seized the throne and the queen. Arthur turns back to a ruin he cannot prevent. The poem gives England an epic, grim Arthur with no magic to save him.
my-days-of-adventure-the-fall-of-france-:
Ernest Alfred Vizetelly recalls the fall of France in 1870 and 1871. His memoir came out in London in 1914. A war poem of his own, The People's War, fronts the book. It calls farmers, sailors, and miners to save wounded France.

The contents move from early memories to the war's outbreak. Then comes the road to revolution in Paris. Vizetelly was there as a young man and saw the collapse. He wrote lives of the French court as well. His tale is firsthand history, vivid on siege, fear, and a nation's fall at the start of a new age.
nightingale-lying-in-institutions-1871:
Introductory Notes on Lying-in Institutions, from 1871, turns Florence Nightingale's methods on childbirth care. Lying-in institutions were hospitals where women gave birth. Nightingale studied their death rates with her usual care for figures. Too many mothers, she found, died from fever after delivery in such places.

The book asks how maternity wards should be built, staffed, and run. Midwifery training receives close treatment, since skill at the bedside decides outcomes. Her mortality statistics were pioneering for the study of childbirth. The Gutenberg text omits the old publisher's catalogue at the end. Readers meet her reform method applied to mothers. The stakes could not be plainer.
openalex-w2011734771:
Roel Aaij and colleagues in the LHCb Collaboration tested a basic rule of particle physics. Their paper appeared in Physical Review Letters in 2014. The rule says electrons and muons should behave alike. The team studied a rare decay of B mesons. Rare decays can reveal new particles.

They used proton collision data from the LHCb detector. They compared decays that produce muons with decays that produce electrons. They measured the ratio of the two decay rates. Their value was the most precise of its kind so far. It agreed with the standard model prediction within stated limits. The result left the basic rule intact for now. It also set a tighter benchmark for future tests.
openalex-w2022905671:
Joshua Galanter, Juan Carlos Fernandez-Lopez, Christopher Gignoux and colleagues built a gene marker panel for ancestry in the Americas. Their paper appeared in PLoS Genetics in 2012. Most people in the Americas have mixed ancestry. Their roots combine Native American, European and African lines. The mix varies a lot between people and groups.

The team selected hundreds of markers that differ between ancestral groups. The panel was tuned for Latin American populations. It estimates each person's ancestral proportions. Such estimates help health studies adjust for ancestry. They also help trace population history. A shared panel lets studies across countries be compared. The work involved labs across the Americas and Spain.
openalex-w2130606571:
Maximiliano Korstanje published this book review in the Jàmbá Journal of Disaster Risk Studies in 2009. He discusses The Risk Society by Ulrich Beck, a landmark work on how modern societies perceive danger. The review grew out of Korstanje's doctoral work on fears of travelling in cities.

Korstanje sums up Beck's claim that today's threats are global and hard for citizens to judge alone. Wealthy groups can hide the side effects of wasteful consumption, while duties and blame blur across borders. Denied risks feed public fear, and markets sell security products in response. Beck's worry centers on environmental harm, above all toxic waste, which forces nations to act together.
openalex-w2156568771:
C. Mark Eakin, Jessica Morgan, Scott Heron, and colleagues published this study in PLoS ONE in 2010. They document the record coral crisis that struck the Caribbean in 2005. Hot ocean water that year caused the most severe bleaching event ever recorded in the basin, killing corals across a wide region.

Satellite tools tracked the warming from June to October and warned managers where stress was building. Those warnings guided when and where field teams surveyed bleaching and death. The field effort surpassed all prior ones in detail and extent. It set a new standard for documenting bleaching damage and for testing the satellite forecasts that reef managers now rely on.
openalex-w2267285071:
Javier Ceja-Navarro, Fernando Vega, Ulaş Karaöz, and colleagues published this study in Nature Communications in 2015. They solved a puzzle about the coffee berry borer, the world's worst coffee pest. Caffeine poisons insects, yet this tiny beetle alone completes its whole life inside the caffeine-rich coffee bean.

Infestations can cut coffee yields by up to four-fifths, and the beetle now lives in most coffee-growing nations. The team shows the secret sits in the beetle's gut. Its resident microbes break down caffeine, detoxifying the diet no other insect can live on. The finding reframes the pest as a partnership between beetle and bacteria, and hints that targeting the microbes could weaken the borer.
openalex-w2553825371:
Houria Djoudi, Bruno Locatelli, and Chloé Vaast, with colleagues, published this 2016 paper in Ambio. It examines how climate change studies handle gender. Climate impacts and adaptation plans affect men and women differently. The authors review forty-one papers on adaptation through the lens of intersectionality, the idea that inequalities overlap and combine.

They find that gender is usually treated as a simple men-versus-women split. Power relations and social and political structures get little attention. This framing paints women mainly as victims, a pattern the authors call the feminization of vulnerability. Intersectional analysis, proven useful elsewhere, has barely entered climate and gender research. Using it, they argue, would reveal people's agency and fairer paths for adaptation. It would also show how climate impacts are shaped by existing power dynamics.
openalex-w2613371971:
Tom Parks, Mariana Mirabel, and Joseph Kado, with colleagues, published this 2017 genetics study in Nature Communications. It searches for inherited factors behind rheumatic heart disease in Oceania. The disease scars heart valves after rheumatic fever and kills many young adults in poorer countries. Pacific islanders carry a particularly heavy burden, yet genetics research had largely overlooked them.

The team ran a genome-wide association study on over three thousand DNA samples. One signal stood out: a common variant in the immunoglobulin heavy chain gene segment IGHV4-61. The risk version changes several amino acids in antibody heavy chains. This is the first genome-wide study of the disease, the authors note. It points to antibody genes as part of how susceptibility is inherited. The finding may also matter for other autoimmune diseases, they suggest.
openalex-w2782974471: Joshua C. Stein, Yeisoo Yu, and Dario Copetti lead the long author list on this 2018 Nature Genetics paper. Its title announces genome sequences for thirteen domesticated and wild relatives in the rice genus Oryza. The preserved sample contains only the author list and institutional affiliations. No abstract, methods, or results survive in the sample. What the comparison found about genetic conservation, turnover, and innovation therefore cannot be stated from the evidence kept here.
openalex-w2904384071:
Simon Roux, Evelien M. Adriaenssens, and Bas E. Dutilh lead a consortium setting standards for uncultivated virus genomes, in Nature Biotechnology. The paper is MIUViG: Minimum Information about an Uncultivated Virus Genome. Metagenomics now recovers viral genomes without growing any virus. These genomes illuminate global viral diversity and virus-host evolution. Reporting quality, however, lagged behind the flood of sequences.

Current genome standards, MISAG and MIMAG, govern single-cell and metagenome microbial genomes. Viral genomes vary too wildly in composition and replication for those rules alone. MIUViG specifies virus-specific checks for completeness, quality, taxonomy, and ecology. It tells authors what details must go with a new uncultivated genome. The Genomic Standards Consortium backs the framework. Shared standards let thousands of viral genomes be compared and trusted. This perspective is the field's rulebook for the metagenomic era.
openalex-w2997096971:
Bernardo Cacho-Díaz, Donovan García-Botello, Talía Wegman-Ostrosky, and colleagues wrote this 2020 review in the Journal of Translational Medicine. It compares the tumor microenvironment of primary cancers with that of their brain metastases. The cancers covered are melanoma, lung cancer, and breast cancer, the main sources of brain metastases.

Most malignant brain tumors are in fact spread from elsewhere in the body. To seed the brain, cancer cells must cross the blood-brain barrier, then reshape their new surroundings to survive. Treatment works better on the primary tumor than on brain deposits, partly because of that barrier. The authors review how the two settings differ, hunting for fresh treatment targets in the brain setting.
openalex-w3156051371:
Marco Necci, Damiano Piovesan, and colleagues report the first Critical Assessment of protein Intrinsic Disorder prediction, or CAID, in Nature Methods in 2021. Some proteins have loose regions with no fixed shape, called intrinsically disordered regions. Computers predict these regions, but nobody had tested the predictors in a fair, blind contest.

The team judged forty-three prediction methods on a shared set of proteins drawn from the DisProt database. The best methods relied on deep learning. The paper sets out how the contest ran and how well each method did. It gives the field a shared benchmark, so new tools can be checked against a known standard.
openalex-w3211488171:
Christina Fitzmaurice and the Global Burden of Disease Cancer Collaboration measured the world cancer burden in JAMA Oncology in 2019. The team tracked twenty-nine cancer groups from 1990 to 2017. For each country they estimated new cases, deaths, years of life lost, and years lived with disability. Cancer control plans need such numbers to set priorities and budgets.

The profiles differed sharply between countries, reflecting varied risk factors, lifestyles, screening, and access to care. Poorer and richer nations often face very different cancer mixes. The authors argue that governments can use these profiles to build fairer national cancer plans. The study remains a standard reference for comparing cancer burden across place and time.
openalex-w4413899071:
Kouki Mikuni, Toshiki Hiraoka, Takumi Kuramoto, and colleagues derive the resonance frequencies of compensated ferrimagnets. Their paper appeared in the Journal of the Physical Society of Japan in 2025. Such magnets hold two opposed magnetic sublattices of unequal strength. At one special temperature, the two cancel and the net magnetism vanishes.

Near that balance point, standard resonance models fail to describe the motion. The authors solve for the resonance frequencies at all temperatures. They treat magnetism pointing in the crystal plane and out of it. Their formulas match optical and light-scattering measurements on real materials. Far from the balance point, the formulas merge with the classic models. One accurate model aids spin-based devices that use these magnets' fast dynamics.
openalex-w7148630071:
