Root shape traits explained part of the leakage in some crops but never all, and no single rule fit every species. It also warns breeders: selecting for richer root leakage may quietly tax yield.
pmc-13437971:
Luigi Del Giudice and co-authors focus a mini-review on the proteins that build the mitochondria's own protein-making machines. Mitochondria carry a small genome and must assemble key energy parts on site, using a private ribosome. Their 2026 paper examines three such proteins in depth: their shapes, jobs, and known links to illness.

Changes in these proteins ripple outward: energy output falls, corrosive oxygen byproducts rise, and quality control for worn mitochondria falters. Neurons, with their huge energy bills and long lives, suffer earliest and worst. The authors propose that these proteins help explain why some tissues fall ill while others are spared in the same disease. They map the open questions, from how each protein behaves in different organs to which ones could be drugged. Their pitch is that a neglected corner of cell biology, the mitochondrial ribosome, may hold fresh entry points for treating degenerative brain disease.
pmc-13438671:
Kelly Rubiano and colleagues gave a job to one of biology's oddest decorations: long strings of asparagine studding a quarter of the malaria parasite's proteins. Plasmodium falciparum owns one of the most lopsided genomes known, rich in letters spelling asparagine, with repeats past a hundred copies. Their function was a standing mystery. Their 2026 study zoomed in on one repeat on PfGCN5, an enzyme tagging histones to loosen DNA.

After the enzyme is cut in the nucleus, its repeat-bearing head stays attached to its tail. Deleting the repeat left the head unstable, and parasites grew poorly, above all under stress. Fine protein measurements showed the repeat steering which histones get tagged. The authors present the first clear function for a poly-asparagine repeat in this parasite. A feature once dismissed as junk turns out to be load-bearing, inviting a second look at other repeats.
pmc-13439271:
Yuntian Gu and a large team attack a classic physics puzzle, the Hubbard model, with neural network wavefunctions, reporting gains in 2026. The model captures electrons that repel each other on a grid and may explain high-temperature superconductors, materials that carry current without loss when fairly warm. Exact answers are out of reach, so computer methods compete on accuracy. The team built transformer-based neural states, borrowing the attention design from language models, plus faster training routines.

Their method reached leading accuracy for the doped two-dimensional model. Curiously, distinct attention heads inside the network each picked up correlations at a different scale, helping the state capture long-range order. Results backed a striped ground state at half filling when a diagonal hopping term was added, matching patterns seen in real cuprate materials.
pmc-13440771:
Sato and colleagues reported in 2026 two cases of burst aneurysms on small collateral arteries in moyamoya disease. In that condition, blocked brain arteries force the growth of a fragile web of backup vessels. Aneurysms on those vessels are common and their rupture carries a grim outlook. Reaching them by catheter is hard because the vessels are tiny and winding.

In the first case, the aneurysm bled again before treatment, and sealing it through a catheter was marred by a rupture during the procedure and fluid buildup in the brain afterward. The second patient had the parent vessel closed off by catheter without complications. The authors weigh the promise and the peril of the approach. Success depends on whether the lesion can be reached safely, so careful mapping of the collateral network must come first.
pmc-13441271:
Wolff and colleagues described in 2026 a 75-year-old woman whose scattered bleeding turned out to be acquired hemophilia A, a rare disorder where the immune system attacks a clotting protein. She arrived with a swollen blood collection under her tongue, blood inside a joint, blood behind an eardrum, and broad bruises, with no past bleeding history.

Blood tests showed one clotting time stretched long while others stayed normal. Mixing her blood with healthy blood did not fix it, a classic sign of an inhibitor. Her factor VIII activity was very low, and the inhibitor was confirmed. Treatment paired a bypassing clotting drug to stop bleeding with steroids and weekly rituximab to wipe out the inhibitor. Within four weeks her clotting tests normalized fully, and the authors stress quick recognition of this rare disorder.
pmc-13441771:
Ashwin Valliyot and colleagues set pregnancy thyroid ranges from a community cohort recruited while newly married in South India, reporting in 2026. Thyroid ranges in pregnancy are usually borrowed from other populations or from women already pregnant. The team recruited 1,507 newly married women aged eighteen to thirty-five, tested thyroid function and antibodies before pregnancy, then followed those who conceived. Only women with normal function and no thyroid antibodies stayed in the reference group.

Four hundred eighty-two pregnancies appeared over eighteen months, and 182 women qualified for the clean reference set. Early thyrotropin ran lower than pre-pregnancy values, then rose slightly later in pregnancy. Standard intervals for thyrotropin and total thyroxine are reported for both trimesters. Early pregnancy thyrotropin tracked with pre-pregnancy levels and waist size. The authors offer locally grounded ranges for judging thyroid results in similar places.
pmc-13442371:
Miso Kim and a large team read charts from twenty-two centres across six countries on advanced melanoma care, mapping which treatments patients received. Anti-PD-1 immune drugs reshaped melanoma care in both after-surgery and advanced settings, yet real-world exposure patterns were uncounted at this scale. An aggregate cohort held 16,260 patients with stage three or four disease from 2018 to 2021. A second cohort of 738 patients received anti-PD-1 therapy and was followed line by line.

Watchful waiting still dominated stage three care after surgery, at over half of patients, while stage four disease drew systemic therapy as standard. Single-agent anti-PD-1 ruled the after-surgery setting almost completely. In advanced disease, single agents and a dual immune pairing split the field. Anti-PD-1 regimens kept reappearing across later treatment lines despite heavy drop-off, and progression was the main reason treatment stopped.
pmc-13442671:
Natalie Smith and colleagues hunt for blood marks that warn of immune side effects from cancer drugs in a 2026 study. The drugs free immune brakes in lung cancer care, yet up to 40 percent of treated people grow inflamed tissue harm. Blood came from 72 people before drug care began, and 23 of them later grew such side effects.

Cell sorting by mass tools covered 59 blood sets, while protein scans and fuel scans each covered 30 sets. Protein scans read more than 10,000 proteins at once in this design. People who later grew side effects showed a distinct cell mix up front, with fewer memory B cells among the shifts. The team hopes such marks can guide care that calms side effects without dulling the anti-tumor push, a balance steroid care now risks.
pmc-13442871:
Xiang Ji and colleagues study grief and job strain in teachers who lost close kin to COVID-19 in a 2026 survey. Replies came from 1,103 high school teachers who bore grief and classroom duty at once. The team asked whether work stress fed deep dread about life and death, and what role burnout and work-home flex played.

Work stress did track with deeper dread in the replies. Burnout carried part of that link, with a 59.3 percent share of the total effect in their model. Four flex types split apart, since only work flex skill changed the stress-burnout link, and it made the link stronger, not weaker. The authors call that flip trauma blocking, where porous work bounds let grief flood the job. They urge schools to guard bounds for bereaved staff.
pmc-13443171:
Young Hwan Kim and colleagues ask whether salt water rinsing cuts return of chronic brain bleeds after drain surgery in a 2026 study. The bleed, a slow pool under the skull, hits older adults often and comes back in many cases. Records covered 126 patients and 145 drain jobs from January 2019 to December 2021.

Bleeds came back in 33 jobs, a share of 22.76 percent of all jobs in the set. The rinse group saw returns at 14.81 percent, well below the no-rinse mark of 27.47 percent in the twin group. Rework rates also fell with rinsing. Male sex, mixed bleed look, and blood thinner use raised return risk. Deep models kept rinsing as a solo guard. The authors back rinsing as a cheap step in drain care.
pmc-13444371:
Junhao Zhang and colleagues track what keeps physical education students on AI learning tools in a 2026 study. Three survey waves ran in April, July, and November 2025, with 511 matched students in the final set. Sport self-belief came first, then tool ease and use views, then lasting use at the end.

All five chained paths in their model held up in the checks. The full chain effect sat at 0.113 points, with a tight trust range in the report. One path through ease, views, and intent gave the largest solo share. Sport confidence thus feeds tool habits through how tools feel to use, step by step. The authors urge PE programs to build sport belief and tool ease in tandem for lasting uptake.
pmc-13444471:
Kitsanapong Kaewbangkerd and colleagues use hard ultrasound to free type II collagen from pig trachea in a 2026 study. Windpipes are a low-value slaughter by-product, yet their cartilage holds prized CII for joint and skin goods. Acid, pepsin, and ultrasound-plus-pepsin routes faced off under tuned terms.

At top terms of 23.75 W per square centimeter for 15 minutes, ultrasound lifted yield to 19.97 percent and cut work time by about 58 percent against classic routes. Acid alone gave just 1.82 percent, mostly the wrong collagen type. The joint route pushed purity to 80.51 percent of the extract. Amino acid marks fit a true CII cast, with glycine thick in the mix. Layer views showed a tight sheet build in the best extract.
pmc-13446271:
Luke A. Fisher and colleagues evolve Escherichia coli in the lab under magnesium chloride stress to find how bacteria learn to bear harsh salts, in a 2026 study. This salt scrambles the structure of biomolecules, unlike table salt, and such brines occur in extreme places on Earth and beyond. Tolerance also matters for industrial fermentations that stall under salt load.

Two evolved strains grew far better in magnesium chloride and in sister harsh salts, but not in table salt. Gene reading tied the gain to faults in a sugar uptake system and in a stress-response switch, plus reshaping of the cell coat. A capsule control system that the parent strain needed for tolerance became needless in the evolved lines, which shows more than one road to resistance.
pmc-13447071:
Jinghua Dai and colleagues test which park scenes best restore calm in older adults, and whether sound helps or hurts, in a 2026 study in Xi'an. Forty-four healthy older adults viewed fourteen scenes from five park types, in silence and with matched sound, while eye trackers and body sensors logged stress signs. Green space is a known balm, yet design rules for aging users run thin.

Scenes with middling plant variety and still water gave the best recovery. Sound did not help across the board: its worth turned on the scene it joined, and rich sound-plus-sight mixes could drag recovery down. Open ground and still water shrugged off distraction well, and sound drew eyes toward water. The authors urge calm planting, quiet water, and soft volume near moving water.
pmc-13447271:
Saurabh Shrivastava and co-authors argue in 2026 that social media influencers shape tooth decay risk in teenagers and young adults. Decay burdens millions and tracks with sugary food and drink. Influencers feel like trusted peers to young followers, so their food promotion carries weight that ordinary adverts may lack.

Direct proof that influencer exposure causes decay is still scarce, the authors concede. The worry runs through behaviour, since exposure links to higher intake of sugary and tooth-harming products. Idealised lifestyles online can normalise those choices during years when identity and habits form. Coordinated action across health, education and platform rules is urged to shrink that digital risk. Longer follow-up studies are also called for to test whether the behaviour path truly ends in more decay.
pmc-13447371:
Aswathi Ram P and colleagues embed iron oxide particles into soft contact lenses in 2026 work toward lenses that also protect the eye. Long lens wear raises risks of infection and inflammation, while drops wash away quickly and rely on patient discipline. Iron oxide particles are cheap, body-friendly and can drive chemical cleaning reactions, making them attractive for a wearable platform.

Particles about eight nanometres wide were mixed evenly into commercial lenses and checked by several imaging and analysis tools. Lenses stayed largely transparent, with computer models showing smaller particles preserve clarity better. At higher loading, lenses broke down a test dye almost fully over two weeks with a helper chemical. Cell tests showed acceptable survival and normal shape, plus activity against a common bacterium and signs of calming inflammation.
pmc-13447571:
Abdurrahman İnkaya and Hasan Güngör report a rare kidney cancer in a nine-year-old liver transplant recipient in a 2026 case study. The cancer type lacks a working metabolic enzyme and is defined by that molecular fault, appearing only occasionally in children. The girl also carried prior lymphoma treatment, immune suppression, high blood pressure and reduced kidney reserve into her care.

Surgeons removed part of the left kidney through open surgery, squeezing local tissue rather than clamping the main vessels to avoid starving the whole kidney of blood. Tissue tests confirmed a low-grade form of the enzyme-deficient cancer, fully removed at an early stage. Kidney function stayed stable afterwards. Inherited gene testing found an uncertain variant, so counselling, reinterpretation over time and long surveillance were arranged.
pmc-13447671:
Tarek Mohamed Abd El-Aziz leads a team uncovering how a kidney salt channel stays anchored at the cell surface in 2026 molecular work. The channel makes the final adjustment to sodium excretion, so its failure causes either salt wasting or high blood pressure from salt retention. Hormone controls were known, while the physical anchoring that keeps active channels in place was not.

A common enzyme tags the channel's beta unit at a conserved site, allowing a scaffold protein to bind and hold the channel at the surface. Breaking either the tag site or the binding motif froze surface movement and cut electrical current sharply in cell tests. Removing the enzyme or scaffold in kidney collecting duct cells, or blocking the enzyme with a drug, abolished channel activity and sped sodium loss in living animals. A new drug target pathway for salt balance is proposed.
pmc-13448171:
You Na Kim, Seulgi You and Joo Sung Sun review imaging of lung tissue and airway injuries after chest trauma in a 2026 article. Bruised or torn lungs and ripped airways can turn life-threatening quickly, and scan findings often decide between watchful care, intensive monitoring and surgery. CT is the central tool, since plain films can lag hours behind the true injury.

Bruising, the commonest lung injury, shows as hazy or dense patches near the impact site and peaks over two to three days before clearing. Tears of the windpipe branches need precise localisation because repair planning depends on the exact site. Severity grading systems for each injury type are summarised with their treatment implications. A clinical checklist and structured report template close the review, aimed at faster, clearer exchanges between radiologists and treating teams.
pmc-13448671:
Ho Jin and colleagues report in 2026 that adding manganese to cadmium selenide quantum dots opens a very fast route for light-driven reduction chemistry. Their experiments show manganese ions catching energy from hot excitons before that energy is lost as heat. A spin flip in the manganese then pushes charge apart and reduces a molecular acceptor.

Using femtosecond laser spectroscopy, the team found electron transfer ran more than ten times faster with manganese present. The pathway worked whether the energy step was uphill or downhill, so spin exchange mattered more than band alignment. The authors argue that magnetic doping could help harvest hot carriers for demanding photocatalytic reactions.
pmc-13448971:
Xincheng Zou and colleagues examine in 2026 how type 2 diabetes shapes recovery after a hip fracture in older adults, using territory-wide Hong Kong health records. They identified 52,472 people aged sixty or older hospitalized for hip fractures between 2011 and 2020, of whom 34.6 percent had diabetes at the time. Follow-up ran through December 2023 for complications, deaths, costs, and further fractures.

Diabetes was independently tied to more heart, kidney, and infection complications during the hospital stay, and to higher one-year mortality, with an adjusted hazard ratio of 1.08, modest but real. Hospital stays lasted no longer, yet costs ran just under five percent higher. Patients whose diabetes had never been diagnosed fared worst of all, with still higher complication and death risks and costs up 24.5 percent across the board. Diabetes did not change rates of bone drug treatment or repeat fracture, leading the authors to press for earlier diagnosis.
pmc-13449371:
Sofia Faraza and colleagues ask in 2026 whether the brain's resting wiring predicts which older adults will carry cognitive training gains into untrained tasks. They analyzed 181 healthy older adults, average age 68, who completed four weeks of cognitive training at three sites in the German AgeGain study, plus 54 controls. Brain scans at rest came before training, and thinking tests ran before, right after, and twelve weeks later.

Most participants did transfer their gains, and the improvement held across the three-month follow-up. Yet baseline connectivity inside two major networks, the default mode network and the central executive network, failed to predict who transferred. Neither seed-based nor component-based analysis found a reliable signal. The authors conclude resting connectivity of large networks is not the marker clinics hope for, and they call for larger, multi-modal imaging studies.
pmc-13449571:
Bhuwan Shrestha and co-authors test in 2026 two drug-free devices for subclinical mastitis on an organic dairy farm, where antibiotics are restricted. They enrolled 129 lactating crossbred cows whose milk cell counts topped 200,000 per milliliter, the standard flag for hidden udder infection. The cows were randomized to acoustic pulse therapy, cold laser therapy, or no treatment. Milk samples before milking tracked cell counts, composition, and bacteria, while herd records supplied yield and removal data.

Cold laser therapy beat the control on bacterial cure, but only in cows with acute, contagious infections. Acoustic pulse therapy tended to lower bacterial counts across the board, whatever the inflammation pattern or history. Neither treatment improved overall recovery, survival, or milk yield in a statistically dependable way. The authors conclude the devices show narrow promise yet fall short of demonstrating lasting benefit for subclinical mastitis under organic rules.
pmc-13449671:
Simon Gray and a large team test in 2026 whether the protein source in the diet, by itself, can drive gut inflammation, using mouse models of colitis. Red meat intake is tied to inflammatory bowel disease flares in people, but the responsible component was unclear. Mice received matched diets built on protein isolates from beef, egg white, casein, soy, or pea, then faced either a chemical colitis trigger or a genetic colitis model.

Beef protein produced the most severe inflammation and pea protein the mildest. The beef effect ran through gut microbes. It shrank two friendly species and let a mucus dweller expand into a thinning mucus layer, and it raised fecal bile acids. Feeding one such acid, taurocholic acid, worsened colitis in pea-fed mice. Adding the fiber psyllium protected beef-fed mice and normalized the bile acid balance, a hint for dietary advice.
pmc-13449771:
Andrea Lin and colleagues warn in 2026 that a common variant in chest anatomy may set patients up for one of tracheostomy's rarest and deadliest complications. The danger is a fistula between the windpipe and the innominate artery. Their single-center series reviews three patients, all sharing a bovine arch, where major arteries branch in a merged pattern, together with an innominate artery riding higher than usual across the trachea. Imaging in each case showed the normal fat cushion between artery and airway had vanished.

Two patients arrived with warning bleeding or early erosion and were saved by prompt surgery with vascular control and tissue placed between the structures. The third arrived with the fistula fully blown and catastrophic bleeding; despite emergency artery tying and airway cleanup, that patient died. The authors urge teams to scan preoperative images for this anatomy and to watch such patients with extra vigilance after tracheostomy.
pmc-13451871:
Tusheng Li and co-authors grade in 2026 how well big AI chat models name rare bone and joint diseases, and whether their hints help doctors. Such diseases are hard to pin down since each is rare and signs vary widely. The team picked 40 of them from China's rare disease list and set four models the same cases.

Three models named the right lead disease in nine of ten cases, while a fourth lagged near two thirds. Doctors at two seniority bands then worked the cases alone, and again with model hints shown as plain advice. Scores after the hints, plus a trust survey, gauge whether AI backup lifts human accuracy without taking the wheel.
pmc-13452271:
Guo and colleagues tested in 2026 whether polyphenols from sea buckthorn berries improve fat metabolism in diabetic obese mice, working through the gut-liver axis. They fed the extract to a genetic obesity mouse model, profiled gut microbes and liver effects, and tested the main compounds in liver cells.

The extract restored healthy HDL cholesterol levels and eased fat buildup in the liver, with a trend toward slower weight gain. pmc-13453071:

pmc-13453471:

Gene profiling showed the transcription factor ZEB2 rose sharply without ADAP. pmc-13453571:

pmc-13453671:

pmc-13454271:

pmc-13456171:

pmc-13456571:

pmc-13457471: Two viburnum plants — sorting out their grouping with chloroplast genomes. Yanlei Liu, Xin Shen, and others compare them. The 2026 Europe PMC paper is plant gene research. pmc-13459271:

pmc-13459371:
Doaa M E Musa and co-authors screened blood donors in Kassala, Sudan, for human herpesvirus 6. pmc-13461071:
LiuGuang Song and co-authors built in 2026 a biomimetic nanoparticle that ferries the steroid dexamethasone into inflamed lungs during sepsis. pmc-13461671:

pmc-13462271:
Dickinson and colleagues probed in 2026, in baker's yeast, how old gene wrap proteins are shared between the two new DNA strands as a cell copies its code. Fate marks ride on crew counts.
pmc-13462671:

pmc-13463371:

pmc-13463671:

pmc-13463971:

pmc-13464071:

pmc-13464971:

pmc-13465171:

pmc-13465371:
Yang and colleagues score food supply security across Gansu Province in this 2026 evaluation study, applying China's broader food security concept that looks beyond grain tonnage alone. pmc-13465671:

pmc-13465871:

pmc-13466271:

pmc-13466471:

pmc-13466971:

pmc-13467571:

pmc-13467671:

pmc-13468271:

pmc-13468571:

pmc-13468671:

pmc-13468871:

pmc-13469471:

pmc-13469671:

pmc-13470371:

pmc-13470771:

pmc-13470971:

pmc-13471171:

pmc-13471271:

pmc-13471371:

pmc-13471471:

pmc-13471571:

pmc-13471671:
Drummond and colleagues developed a simpler exam format, the Probabilistic Reasoning Test, to judge whether medical students reason soundly about doubt in clinical cases. Their 2026 validation study gave 575 participants, 538 fifth-year students plus 19 residents and 18 pediatricians, matched sets of the new test, script concordance tests, and multiple-choice questions on the same cases.

The new format tracked the established one closely, with 91.4% agreement between responses and a weighted kappa of 0.91 across the comparison. Students liked it far better: 90% of participants preferred it over the script concordance format for examinations. Its weakness was telling groups apart, since scores did not significantly separate students from residents and senior pediatricians, so the authors back it for undergraduate teaching, not expertise ranking.
pmc-13472571:
Ye and colleagues report in 2026 a new genetic cause of Stickler syndrome, a connective tissue disorder affecting eyes, joints, and the face, in a five-year-old Chinese girl. Whole-exome sequencing found two previously unreported variants in the gene LOXL3. One came from each parent, and family testing confirmed the pattern.

Computer simulations of the altered protein showed one variant loosens its structure and exposes more of it to water. It also disrupts a pocket that binds copper, which the protein needs to work. The child had early severe short-sightedness, a cleft palate, and an underdeveloped central retina. A review of earlier LOXL3 cases found high myopia the most common feature. The authors say the findings widen the known spectrum of this rare syndrome.
pmc-13474371:
G. A. Gerasimov reviews new global guidance in 2026 on adding iodine to salt to protect public health. Iodized salt now reaches most of the world, and 126 states require it by law. The share of people using iodized salt sits near nine in ten worldwide. Just over one hundred states now show enough iodine in diets, a sharp turn from the early 1990s.

The review walks through six briefing notes that update how programs run and how they are checked. One note urges folding iodine checks into broader health surveys to save cost and effort. Collecting urine samples at routine pregnancy visits is raised as a cheaper watch method. Health planners gain fresh options for keeping gains in place.
pmc-13474571:
Hunter J Weaver and colleagues test how a stress hormone calms inflammation in mice in 2026, with or without broken sleep. Broken sleep is known to raise inflammatory signals in brain and body. Mice had hormone glands removed, no surgery, or hormone replaced at high dose in drinking water. Gene activity for two inflammatory signals was read across brain and body tissues.

High-dose hormone strongly cut inflammatory gene activity in most tissues, beating both other groups. Gland removal alone raised activity only slightly and only in a few spots. Broken sleep added little once hormone level was accounted for. Dose and tissue type, more than sleep loss, set the inflammatory tone in this test.
pmc-13474771:
Liu and co-authors 3D-printed a bone scaffold from carbonate hydroxyapatite, the mineral family real bone is built from. They doped it with terbium, a rare-earth element, to speed regeneration of jaw and skull defects. Their 2026 study tested the printed scaffold's strength, breakdown, and cell friendliness, then implanted it in rat skull defects.

In culture the doped scaffold outperformed plain and carbonate-only versions, raising pre-osteoblast proliferation by 6 to 30% by day five and driving stronger bone-differentiation signals across staining and protein assays. In the rats it grew robust new bone and blood vessels in the defects, and organ checks across heart, liver, spleen, lung, and kidney found no toxic side effects from the terbium. The authors present the material as a first proof that rare-earth doping belongs in bone tissue engineering.
pmc-13474871:
Lan Sun and co-authors test forward-looking nursing in 2026 for women waking from general anesthesia after gynecologic surgery. Forward-looking, or feedforward, care plans for risks before they arise rather than reacting after. A total of 130 patients split into routine care and the added forward-looking plan. Waking scores, event counts, and satisfaction were compared.

The forward-looking group had fewer complications and fewer nursing adverse events overall. Breathing return, tube removal, and full waking all came faster there. Waking scores at entry matched between groups, so the gap grew during recovery itself. Satisfaction also ran higher with the planned approach.
pmc-13474971:
Chen and colleagues checked whether two advanced MRI methods give steady, repeatable readings at 5 tesla, a very strong scanner field, in 2026. The methods, called APT and GluCEST, sense proteins and the brain chemical glutamate through proton exchange with water. The team tested them on lab phantoms at varied acidity and protein levels, then scanned 96 patients with brain tumors and compared tumor, swelling, and healthy regions.

In phantoms, both methods repeated almost exactly, with agreement scores above 0.96 across sessions and days in the validation work. In patients, two readers agreed excellently as well, with scores above 0.93 for tumor and surrounding tissue measurements. Aggressive gliomas read higher than slower ones, and a GluCEST change ratio separated the grades best, scoring 0.846 on the standard accuracy curve, supporting the scans for tumor grading work.
pmc-13475271:
Calcagno and co-authors hunted for pressure readings that warn of trouble during urgent ablation for ventricular tachycardia, a dangerous fast rhythm, in 2026. They reviewed 102 patients rushed in for the procedure who had also had a heart catheter study within the prior year. Two right-heart indices were tested: a ratio of right atrial to left-sided filling pressure, and a pulsatility index for the lung artery.

Two-thirds of the patients, 67 of the 102, arrived in VT storm, meaning repeated episodes, and 47 percent had very weak heart pumping. A pressure ratio above 0.6 independently predicted kidney injury, at odds of 10.4 times the lower group, and predicted blood pressure instability during the procedure as well. The pulsatility index, by contrast, predicted nothing, and neither did a low pumping fraction, so the authors recommend adding the simple ratio to pre-procedure risk checks.
pmc-13476071:
Sun and colleagues reported in 2026 on the Fourth Westlake Symposium on AI Proteomics and Virtual Cell, held at Westlake University in Hangzhou in October 2025. Artificial intelligence is reshaping proteomics, the large-scale study of proteins, by sharpening identification and counting from mass spectrometry data, mapping protein interactions, and joining data across omics layers. The shared long-term aim is the AI virtual cell, a model that captures a cell's inner dynamics to forecast disease and guide drug design.

Invited leaders from experiment and computation traded views across two days. Speakers stressed that better instruments plus AI reading of spectra are deepening and sharpening protein measurement. Sessions ranged over spatial and time-resolved protein analysis and the joining of many data types. The report frames the virtual cell as a collective project needing exactly this mix of skills, and records the field's shared agenda as it stood at the meeting.
pmc-13477271:
Mumtaz Begum and colleagues published a 2026 population study from South Australia on how children born with heart defects are developing when they start school. The team linked school-entry development checks with birth and perinatal records covering 2002 to 2014. Children with diagnosed syndromes or chromosome conditions were left out of the analysis.

Among nearly 68,000 singleton children, 656 had a heart defect. Those children more often had special needs or at least one area of developmental weakness than children without a defect. The higher risk appeared in severe cases and in milder cases alike. The authors say development checks and early support should reach every child with a heart defect, not only those who had early surgery.
pmc-13479571:
Raymond L. Blaha and colleagues published a 2026 study using deep learning on deer movement data to flag chronic wasting disease, a fatal prion illness of deer and elk. Infected animals can look healthy for months, so behavior change might betray infection before symptoms. GPS collar records from free-ranging mule deer provided the raw material.

Unsupervised autoencoder models, trained to recognize normal movement, spotted anomalous animals with at least 84 percent accuracy and 89 percent precision. Speed, direction, and path winding measures mattered most in separating infected from healthy deer. A supervised variant performed differently, a contrast the authors examine. Wildlife managers could use such screening to focus testing and culling where collars already track herds.
pmc-13479971:
Samira Sadat Pourhosseini and coauthors published a 2026 interview study of gaps in mental health and mind-and-social support during disasters in Iran. Weak support systems leave people with lasting harm, alone and as a group. Twenty experts in mental health, disaster work, and health policy were questioned in December 2024, picked on purpose for their roles.

Guided sorting of their accounts split the problems into structure, process, and resource groups. Experts told of unclear duties, thin trained crews, funding that arrives late, and services that vanish once cameras leave. Their fixes target each gap, from standing rosters of trained helpers to protected budget lines. The authors aim to move Iranian disaster planning from ad-hoc kindness to a planned, organized support response.
pmc-13480071:
Abou Abdallah Malick Diouara and colleagues present a 2026 study of past COVID exposure among pregnant women in Senegal. The team tested stored blood samples from 1,227 women who attended pregnancy clinics from March to July 2021, in the Delta wave period. Samples came from five sites, two in Dakar and one each in three regional capitals.

About sixty-five percent of women carried antibodies showing past infection, a share far above the count of reported cases at the time. Rates ran highest in Dakar and Ziguinchor, though gaps between sites did not reach statistical weight. Age made little difference, with all groups near two in three positive. The results show the virus spread widely through this group while formal case counts stayed low, a pattern the authors note matches findings elsewhere in Africa.
pmc-13480471:
Drijver-Headley and colleagues compared in 2026 how frailty, the slow loss of strength and reserve with age, plays out across seventeen lands. They drew on five matched ageing surveys that span the United States, Europe, China, and Mexico. A shared index counted thirty one health deficits for each person, from ills to lost tasks. The team then tracked deaths and new deficits over four years, with a side look at near fit people, named the zero state group.

Frailty ran highest in the United States, Mexico, and the south and east of Europe. It ran lowest in the north and center of Europe. Mexico showed the most deaths and the fastest pile up of new deficits. Swiss and Nordic groups showed the least of both. The near fit lens split lands more sharply, but with weaker stats. The authors warn it can hide gaps inside each land.
pmc-13482371:
Mahdizadeh and colleagues build a cleanup system in 2026 for tetracycline, a stubborn antibiotic that escapes farms and drug factories into waterways. Their reactor couples microelectrolysis, tiny iron-carbon galvanic cells that attack pollutants, with a layered catalyst coated in titanium dioxide and ultraviolet light. A statistical design method tuned the settings, testing acidity, contact time, drug concentration, and the carbon to iron ratio together.

The catalyst particles came out uniform at about 50 nanometers across, and the tuned microelectrolysis alone removed 97 percent of the drug at its best settings in the optimization runs. Adding catalyst and ultraviolet light pushed removal to 98 percent even at a high starting concentration of 100 milligrams per liter within 55 minutes of treatment. That beat the plainer systems clearly, microelectrolysis alone at 62 percent, catalyst alone at 85 percent, and catalyst without light at 93 percent overall.
pmc-13482471:
Liu and colleagues profile 138 cases of classic adrenocortical carcinoma in 2026, a rare and aggressive adrenal gland cancer, treated at Peking Union Medical College Hospital across four decades. Chinese data on the disease are thin, so the team combined their 1984 to 2024 case records with gene expression profiles from 79 patients in an international cancer database. They charted who gets the disease, how it presents, and which markers track survival.

Women outnumbered men, most patients were diagnosed past 40, and tumors favored the right gland at 1.28 times the left side's rate in the cohort. The median tumor measured 9.05 centimeters across at diagnosis, and the growth marker Ki-67 ran high, with a median of 20 percent of cells staining positive. Advanced stage came with higher Ki-67, and higher Ki-67 in tissue or gene form predicted worse survival, with fast-growing tumors enriched for cell cycle and p53 pathway genes.
pmc-13483471:
Puxian Fang and co-authors report a 2026 study pinning down which part of a host protein coronaviruses cannot do without. The protein, TMEM41B, aids many coronaviruses, yet deleting it outright kills mouse embryos, blocking plans for virus-proof farm animals. Working with a pig deltacoronavirus that can also infect people, the team cut the protein into pieces to find the vital stretch.

The virus needed the protein while copying itself, not while entering or leaving cells. One segment, the sixth membrane span, proved essential alongside a known core region. Mice bred without just that span resisted a mouse coronavirus, suffered less liver damage, and survived better. Trimming one small span may thus yield animals that shrug off coronaviruses while keeping the protein's day job intact.
pmc-13483571:
Zhicheng Ke leads a 2026 study asking whether a blood microRNA combined with bedside lung ultrasound can diagnose acute lung injury more accurately. Blood levels of miR-769-5p, a small regulatory RNA, were measured in patients alongside ultrasound scores of the lungs. Cell experiments with lung-type cells exposed to bacterial toxin tested how the marker affects inflammation signals.

Patients with lung injury showed lower blood levels of the marker than comparison groups. Pairing the blood test with the ultrasound score improved diagnostic accuracy beyond either measure alone, and both measures tracked with injury risk. In cells, raising the marker reduced inflammatory signaling, reactive oxygen output, and cell death. The combined approach may help clinicians confirm a dangerous and hard-to-pin-down lung condition sooner.
pmc-13483671:
Fanrou Zhang and colleagues design a nanoparticle treatment aimed at the mitochondrial stress that fuels gum disease. Their 2026 study builds ceria particles, a known antioxidant material, tuned with ruthenium in different arrangements. The goal combines two jobs, mopping up harmful reactive oxygen inside cells and capturing mitochondrial DNA that leaks out and triggers inflammation.

A middle arrangement using tiny ruthenium clusters beat both single-atom and larger-particle versions on enzyme-like activity and immune calming. The clusters also raised positive surface charge, which helped the particles bind the leaked DNA by electrical attraction. In rats with induced gum disease, local treatment eased gum inflammation and suppressed inflammatory activity. Size and structure tuning therefore decided how well one particle could do both jobs at once.
pmc-13486371:
Machado and colleagues published a 2026 study on what Brazilians know about sepsis across a decade. Sepsis, the body's runaway response to infection, kills hundreds of thousands in Brazil yearly. Early recognition by the public speeds care, yet awareness has lagged. The team compared three national surveys of lay people over time.

Awareness of sepsis improved substantially across the survey years in Brazil. Still, large knowledge gaps remained at the end of the period. Schooling and income shaped awareness more than almost any other trait. People who had met sepsis through family illness also knew more. The authors urge campaigns aimed squarely at lower-income audiences next. Brazil counts roughly 240,000 adult sepsis deaths in intensive care yearly.
pmc-13486471:
Emami-Karvani and co-authors isolated a bacterium from oil refinery sludge that both eats iron and desalts water inside a microbial fuel-cell device. The strain, Advenella faeciporci ZF1, tolerates heavy iron doses that would kill most microbes. Their 2026 study placed it in a three-chamber desalination cell fed with real refinery brine, where bacterial electricity nudges salt ions out of the middle chamber.

Over fifteen days the cell removed about 71 percent of sodium and about 79 percent of calcium from the brine tested. Chloride removal was weaker, at about 28 percent over the same run. At moderate salinity the device produced a peak voltage near 410 millivolts within 48 hours of operation. The bacterium also stored energy-rich granules and showed magnetic sensing behavior. Emami-Karvani proposes it for combined desalination and cleanup of metal-laden industrial wastewater.
pmc-13486671:
Matti Gärtner tests if a shift in dopamine signals changes blood flow in a brain reward hub in depression. Loss of joy is a core sign of major depression, and it ties to weak dopamine action. In this 2026 trial, 111 people took part: 57 with major depression and 54 healthy peers. Each got one low dose of amisulpride, a dopamine blocker, or a dummy pill. No one knew who got which.

The drug raised blood flow in the ventral striatum, the hub in focus, in both groups. No other reward area changed in a firm way. Flow in that hub tracked self-rated loss of joy. One right frontal gap seen on dummy pills faded on the drug. One dose can't treat depression, but the scan gives a clean target to aim at.
pmc-13487171:
Yun Zhang sorts dialysis patients by how tied in they feel with other people. No past study had mapped this spread for people on long-term dialysis. This 2026 study enrolled 365 patients at a large hospital in Anhui, China. In the end, 345 valid forms came back. Scales scored felt ties, social support, and bounce-back strength.

Three groups came out of the data. Low felt ties held 31.9 percent of patients. Mid ties held 42.3 percent, and high ties held 25.8 percent. School level, job state, and dialysis shift each helped set group place. Illness load, bounce-back strength, and support levels played parts too. Dialysis eats much of a patient's week for years. Early checks can point tie-building help to the third who start most cut off.
pmc-13487571:
Boyang Zhou pools trial evidence on a drug class used alone for adult eczema, separating skin-applied from swallowed versions. Published in 2026, the systematic review and meta-analysis gathers five studies of phosphodiesterase-4 inhibitor monotherapy in atopic dermatitis. Quality grading uses a standard observational scale, and pooling runs in dedicated review software.

Topical versions cut eczema severity scores significantly by four weeks and held the gain at twelve weeks, with fewer overall side effects than comparison care. Swallowed versions cut scores progressively more through sixteen weeks and beyond, yet raised systemic side effects significantly. Target lesion severity also fell quickly under topical treatment. Route therefore decides the trade, since creams offer gentler safety while pills offer deeper effect at higher cost to tolerability.
pmc-13487671:
Wong and the editors of Australian Prescriber prepared a short drug comment in 2026 on elafibranor, sold as Iqirvo. The drug treats primary biliary cholangitis, a slow liver disease that harms the small bile ducts. It is meant for adults who gain too little from the usual first drug, ursodeoxycholic acid, or who cannot take that drug at all.

Elafibranor turns on two cell switches, called PPAR-alpha and PPAR-delta, that help control bile acids, swelling, and scar growth in the liver. In the ELATIVE trial, about half of the treated patients met the blood test goal at one year. Very few on placebo did so, and gains showed within four weeks. Common side effects were gut pain, loose stools, and nausea, mostly mild in grade.
pmc-13488571:
Mohammad Alshaban and co-authors study sleep problems in autistic children in Jordan in a 2026 survey. Parents of more than five hundred children filled in a standard sleep form. The children were aged two to fourteen, and most were boys. Poor sleep was very common in this group. Many children fought bedtime, woke in the night, or slept too few hours.

Sleep was worse in children who also had epilepsy, a brain condition that causes seizures. Age and sex made little difference in the scores. The team adjusted the counts for these factors and still found the same pattern. They advise doctors to ask about sleep at each visit and to treat seizures with care, since both shape how well a child rests.
pmc-13491671:
Wenjing Ma and four co-authors gather in 2026 every known case of a rare intestinal cancer defined by loss of the SMARCA4 gene switch. The tumor grows as sheets of undifferentiated cells, lacks any standard treatment, and usually kills quickly. The team adds two new patients to eighteen published cases and summarizes the combined picture.

Four in five patients were men, with an average age of fifty-six, and tumors often showed dead tissue and rapid cell division under the microscope. Staining confirmed SMARCA4 loss in every case, and spread to distant organs was already present in about two of five patients at diagnosis. Median survival was eleven months, and chemotherapy helped little. Two patients, though, stayed in complete remission beyond eighteen months on the immune drug pembrolizumab.
pmc-13493771:
Tulyakanit and co-authors compare two operations for involutional entropion, an age-related condition where the lower eyelid turns inward and lashes rub the eye. Both operations add a lateral tarsal strip, a tightening step at the eyelid's outer corner, but differ in how they fix the muscles that hold the lid out. The 2026 review covers 155 patients treated at two Thai hospitals, with 184 eyes operated on and follow-up averaging just over three years.

Success rates were nearly identical, at just above nine in ten eyes for both procedures on the authors' figures. The Wies operation was quicker, taking about 68 minutes per eye against roughly 83 minutes for the Jones approach in the operating room data. Outcomes diverged by surgeon experience: trainees matched consultants with the Wies method but did notably worse with the Jones method. The authors suggest the quicker operation suits older patients and training settings.
pmc-13493871:
Wang Xin and four colleagues combine gene data and machine learning in 2026 to find the scaffolding genes that matter most in diabetic retinopathy. The disease thickens the retina's basement membranes early on, a remodeling of the extracellular matrix, the protein mesh between cells. Overlapping diabetes and eye-disease gene lists with a matrix database produced nine candidate genes.

Six learning algorithms raced to classify patients, and the Extra Trees model won. Five genes survived importance testing, including SFRP1, FN1, and ECM2, and their expression patterns shifted distinctly from healthy to diabetic to eye-diseased samples. The genes tied into nerve-related pathways and tracked with several immune cell types in the tissue. Regulatory networks and drug databases then connected the five to candidate medicines, sketching future treatment leads.
pmc-13493971:
Awj Twam leads a sixteen-author team testing in 2026 whether a computer can grade liver cancer risk from MRI scans with no human outlining at all. Clinicians normally trace tumors by hand before computing enhancement pattern maps, voxel level fingerprints of how contrast washes through tissue. A lightweight network called PocketNet took over the tracing, and its output fed the same risk analysis.

Human experts disagreeing with each other set the realistic accuracy ceiling, and the machine approached it for larger tumors while lagging on small ones. Reassuringly, risk predictions from machine outlines matched those from hand-drawn ones, because the enhancement fingerprints tolerate wobbly borders. A fully automated biomarker could slot into surveillance programs for high risk patients without adding radiologist hours.
pmc-13494071:
Bollemeijer and colleagues compare two ways of treating severely malnourished children in Jowhar, Somalia: standard facility-based feeding programmes versus village health workers treating children in their villages. World Health Organization guidance allows the village option, but solid evidence has been thin. Their 2026 study enrolled 1,183 children with uncomplicated severe malnutrition during the first months of 2024, split between two facility sites and eight villages, all receiving therapeutic food and weekly checks.

Recovery rates came out nearly equal, with the village group just a shade behind on raw proportions, and adjusted analyses found no difference in weight gain. Children reached by village workers arrived less severely depleted, suggesting earlier detection, and they finished treatment sooner, easing the burden on families. The facility children had started out worse on both arm circumference and weight-for-height measures. The authors back expanding the village model in hard-to-reach areas of Somalia.
pmc-13495171:
Marianne Richaud and colleagues report, in a 2026 study, that DNA floating free in blood carries a record of how it was wrapped in the cell, and that cancer changes the pattern. Such fragments come mostly from blood cells and survive because they ride on nucleosomes, the spools DNA winds around. The team pulled fragment maps from a public database for healthy people and cancer patients.

They found that how fully a spool site is occupied tracks with how tightly DNA binds there, shown by coding patterns and fragment sizes. Occupancy also split cleanly between healthy and cancer samples, and a learning model told seven cancer types from health with high scores on both sensitivity and specificity. Cancer shifted the pattern body-wide, yet each type kept its own marks. The authors offer the readout both as basic insight into blood DNA and as a base for blood-based cancer tests.
pmc-13495371:
Hermel and Saven reported the Scripps regimen in 2026, a low-dose pairing of vemurafenib with rituximab for hairy cell leukemia, a rare slow-growing blood cancer. Standard drugs cure many patients but crush blood counts and immunity, and the usual vemurafenib dose often forces dose cuts without lasting control. Their pilot used a quarter-strength vemurafenib dose for a fixed period alongside the antibody rituximab in fifteen patients, both newly diagnosed and relapsed.

Every patient reached a complete blood count recovery. The overall response rate was 87 percent, with about three in four reaching complete remission and just over half clearing measurable residual disease. Blood counts recovered over one to two months, and the lack of heavy marrow suppression contrasted well with older therapy. Results looked similar in new and previously treated patients. The authors call the regimen a lower-toxicity option that deserves testing in larger prospective studies.
pmc-13498571:
Linzhi Yin and colleagues present in 2026 a computer model that predicts how the inner structure of a common aluminium grade changes during cold rolling. Lab checks and a cost study accompany the model. Rolling thinner strengthens the metal through tiny crystal defects called dislocations, and tracking their density helps explain grain refinement, meaning the shrinking of metal crystals. The work also weighs use of this aluminium in lithium-ion battery parts.

Simulations covered thickness cuts from light to severe, run inside standard engineering software with a custom material routine. Heavier cuts raised plastic strain and refined grains most near surfaces and edges, while defect density rose fast then levelled off. X-ray checks at two mid-level cuts matched predictions closely. Their cost analysis favoured this grade over two rivals across a ten-year view.
pmc-13501571:
Hamza Jawad leads a six-author team reporting a 2026 genome study of sheep that resist the blood-feeding worm Haemonchus contortus, a parasite whose drug resistance is growing. The team infected 32 Rideau Arcott ewe lambs and counted worm eggs in their droppings at five time points. Sixteen animals showed consistent extreme responses: nine resistant and seven susceptible. Whole genome sequencing at moderate coverage then searched for copy number variations, stretches of DNA that are duplicated or deleted.

Resistant lambs carried far fewer eggs, about 10.5-fold lower at day 21 and three- to fourteen-fold lower later. Combining three detection algorithms yielded 22,184 high-confidence variants grouped into 3,751 regions covering 2.63 percent of the genome. One 2.3 megabase duplication containing the mucus-related gene CLCA1 appeared only in resistant sheep, which also held many more gene gains overall. Susceptible sheep showed duplications tied to metabolic problems. The findings offer targets for breeding parasite-resistant flocks.
pmc-13501671:
Sopak Supakul leads a six-author team presenting a 2026 review of how human pluripotent stem cells are used to model the striatum, a brain region central to movement, reward, and habit. Animal models mislead here because cell makeup, timing, and wiring differ between species. The review covers methods for coaxing embryonic and induced pluripotent stem cells into striatal cell types, above all the medium spiny neurons that form the region's main output. Patterning with small molecules, direct transcription factor induction, and three-dimensional organoid and assembloid cultures all feature.

Human medium spiny neurons mature slowly, a trait the authors link to specifically human disease vulnerability. Most disease modelling so far concerns Huntington's disease, where the models exposed early developmental, synaptic, and network faults. Newer work extends to other conditions and to cortico-striatal assembloids that join two brain regions. Remaining gaps include incomplete maturation and missing non-neuronal cell types.
pmc-13501871:
Mohamed Suhail Mohamed Nabi leads a seven-author team with a 2026 narrative review of congenital heart disease in children, spanning early detection, treatment, and life after repair. The team searched PubMed, Scopus, Web of Science, and Google Scholar for work published from 2015 to 2026, including studies, reviews, and guidelines on diagnosis, survival, development, and quality of life. The conditions range from small septal holes that may close alone to blue, duct-dependent lesions needing treatment within hours of birth.

The review walks the care pathway: prenatal ultrasound and fetal heart scanning, newborn pulse screening, confirmatory heart ultrasound, steadying medicines, catheter procedures, open surgery, and intensive care, followed by structured lifelong follow-up. Survival has improved greatly, yet survivors still face leftover lesions, rhythm problems, lung pressure disease, growth and learning delays, and repeat procedures. The authors argue that early detection, fast referral, lesion-specific planning, and permanent team surveillance decide outcomes.
pmc-13501971:
Richard B. Yapi and six colleagues published this 2026 pilot study on teaching human and animal health workers together to fight brucellosis in Côte d'Ivoire, where the bacterial zoonosis is under-recognised in human medicine. First, a March 2024 survey of 54 professionals in the Hambol region measured baseline knowledge. Then the team designed a one-day interprofessional workshop and ran it in February 2025 with 22 participants from medical, veterinary and public health institutions, testing knowledge before and after.

At baseline, 91 percent of respondents knew of zoonoses, but only 39 percent could identify brucellosis, and nobody named it as a cause of fever or miscarriage. Veterinarians were far more aware, at about 81 percent, than human healthcare workers at about 23 percent. After training, overall knowledge scores rose from 34.5 to 37.0, and symptom recognition improved. Diagnosis and control knowledge did not budge. The authors call joint training feasible and promising, while asking for larger, longer studies.
pmc-13503871:
Shengjian Liang leads a team that imaged how a childhood lung virus locks onto human cells, in a 2026 study. The virus, enterovirus D68, can cause severe chest illness and a polio-like weakness in children. A cell protein named MFSD6 serves as its main door into airway cells.

Sharp microscope images show the virus bound to a loop of that protein, for both an old strain and a current one. One part of the loop plugs into a single virus coat unit, while a sugar chain on the loop grips the next unit over. That sugar contact pops out a fatty plug inside the virus and loosens it, priming it to infect. The two-part grip may stop the virus from opening too early.
pmc-13504771:
Miguel A. Quiroz-Reyes leads a team reviewing how surgeons pick filler materials that hold the retina in place after eye surgery, in a 2026 paper. Choices include air, gases, silicone oils, and heavy liquids. Each floats or sinks and grips the eye wall in its own way.

The review ties those physical traits to where the retina tore and how complex the case is. Light fillers support the upper retina; heavy ones prop up the lower part. For simple detachments and many macular holes, air or a short-lived gas works well with less pressure trouble. Heavy oils and staged heavy liquids suit giant tears low in the eye, though proof is mostly observational. Gel-based stand-ins for the eye's natural jelly remain experimental.
pmc-13505171:
Berceste Guler Ayyildiz, Halil Ayyildiz, and Tolga Fikret Tözüm compared two kinds of membrane used when dentists widen a thin jaw ridge before placing implants. One type dissolves over time and the other does not. Working from records and paired three-dimensional scans taken before and after treatment, they measured ridge width, height, and shape at several depths.

Horizontal bone change did not differ clearly between the membrane types at any level measured. How the membrane was fixed in place, the starting ridge angle, and the thickness of the tongue-side bone plate did shape bone change near the crest. Starting concavity depth and top bone thickness also linked with bone gain, though each unit change mattered only slightly. The authors stress careful scan-based planning before surgery, and they ask for prospective studies with more even patient groups.
pmc-13505371:
Masaki Okamura and colleagues present a cheap handheld way to measure the average tilt of leaves across a whole crop canopy. Leaf angle shapes how sunlight feeds the canopy, yet measuring it well has usually needed costly gear or slow leaf-by-leaf work. Their tool is a small stereo depth camera held level above the crop, taking colour and depth pictures that simple geometry turns into an average angle.

Tests against a board set at known angles and against single leaves checked with a digital level confirmed the readings. The method's average angle also matched a similar trait from a far pricier canopy analyser. Field trials separated rice, barley, soybean, and wheat by variety, growth stage, and planting density. Because the kit is light, fast, and inexpensive, the authors expect field researchers without sensing expertise to adopt it readily.
pmc-13507271:
Weiqiu Liang leads a 2026 team that brings nickel catalysis into radiation chemistry to tame its wild radical mixtures. Ionizing radiation splits molecules into many reactive radicals at once, which usually couples them into messy byproducts. Borrowing from light-driven metal chemistry, the team let nickel corral those radicals into chosen pathways.

For carbon-hydrogen arylation, a reaction attaching ring groups to carbon skeletons, yields jumped from under five percent to as high as 82 percent. No light sensitizers were needed, and light-sensitive starting materials survived. Chiral ligands, handed helper molecules, even steered the reaction toward one mirror-image product with strong excess. Radiation-driven synthesis gains selectivity long thought out of reach.
pmc-13508271:
Balveer Saini and Dinesh Kumar Saini present a smart staffing system that adjusts hospital worker levels to live patient demand, in 2026 work. Hospitals face rising costs and demand with fixed rosters that cannot flex at busy hours. Their model blends fuzzy logic, which handles vague inputs like urgency grades, with a genetic algorithm that searches for better rosters. It was tested in simulations modeled on a multi-specialty hospital in Jaipur, India. The system watches queues across several service points at once.

Simulations showed peak-hour waiting times fell by nearly three quarters after the fuzzy logic changes. The genetic search then cut average waiting time by about half compared with fixed staffing. Stress tests showed the model coped well when sudden surges hit the system. The authors argue that live staffing control could trim waits and use scarce staff better, in place of rosters set once and left unchanged.
pmc-13508371:
Jakub Helvich and six co-authors study how teen activities change the web of links among mental health, substance use, and problem social media use, in 2026 work. Data came from a 2022 national school survey in Czechia covering 14,588 adolescents with an average age under fourteen. Network models mapped how heavy social media use, mood symptoms, drinking and smoking, and pastimes connect. Separate networks were built for each pastime type, from solo sports to arts and community groups, and then compared.

When solo sports entered the model, the link between drinking and problem social media use vanished. Community activities and solo sports each softened some conflict and escape links around social media. Only sports tied to less loss of interest in pastimes from social media, with solo sports strongest. Community activities, by contrast, linked to more deception and family conflict around use.
pmc-13511371:
